About this guide Systemic investing is an emergent response to the challenges of our time. It is an approach to capital deployment that seeks to transform systems to produce the best longterm outcomes for people and the planet. This approach is crystalizing because it is increasingly evident that conventional approaches to investing are limited in their ability to effectively address pressing ecological and social issues, and the economic risks and opportunities they present. This is a guide for investors who are serious about driving systemic solutions, offering investors an accessible introduction to systemic investing. Drawn together as a community effort based on literature, interviews, and field work, the guide outlines key concepts and tools, as well as providing case studies and actionable first steps.

Foreword

Dr. Falko Paetzold Founder and CEO Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth

Seth Fleisher Managing Director Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth, Americas

Dr. Jason Jay Director MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative

Dominic Hofstetter Executive Director TransCap Initiative

Alexandra (Alie) Korijn Managing Director TWIST

Sam Bonsey Executive Director The ImPact

Now is the right time for private wealth holders to take systemic action, and the body of knowledge and practice that has emerged - if synthesised properly is well-positioned to guide the way. Why now? The challenges of our time are interconnected, and so are the solutions. Systems thinking tools can yield strong portfolios and outsized impact. Once understood, you can’t not first think about the underlying systems. Why wouldn’t you consider connections and leverage points before deploying capital? This is the “systems turn” that we are observing and describing in this guide. We believe that it can change the world. How? CSP has built a reputation as a translator of cutting-edge research and practice for the private wealth audience. The process is a continuously spinning flywheel of trainings and publications. This guide draws from and feeds into trainings, allowing investors of all backgrounds to grasp the key frameworks and implement them in their own setups. Who? A core value of us collectively is “radical collaboration”—to work deeply together to advance meaningful impact. This guide is exemplary of that: we developed it together as a true community effort to provide a solid platform for actors ready to engage in systemic investing. Let’s get started—toward impact!

Systemic investing is an emerging approach to deploying capital that is used to address complex ecological and social issues. It evolved from introducing systems thinking to impact investing, shifting the focus from targeting specific outcomes through “point solutions”to transforming the underlying systems that generate those outcomes.

Systemic investing adds value by identifying leverage points for targeted interventions, enabling synergistic investments across asset classes through“strategic portfolios.” The approach uses systems thinking to help investors see the world’s greatest challenges as interconnected systems rather than linear problems. System Maps

Integration

A key tool in systemic investing is the system map, which visually depicts connections between elements, enabling a cocreated understanding of the system and uncovering leverage points for outsized systemic impact. Systems mapping relies on setting boundaries along geographic, issue, and sector dimensions, which also provides a means to manage complexity and define a space for action.

A portfolio-level view involves the synergistic deployment of capital for systems transformation. The resources invested encompass commercial investments, catalytic investments, philanthropy, and other forms of“capital”such as reputation or expertise. In terms of portfolio management, this change represents a shift from a riskreturn approach to one based on synergies-return optimization.

This guide provides wealth holders with an understanding of systemic investing and practical steps to begin their own journey.

Getting started

Case Studies

Collaboration

For those looking to get started in systemic investing, we introduce four steps: 1. Defining system boundaries 2. Understanding the system 3. Identifying your potential role 4. Testing a portfolio strategy that leverages synergies across asset classes We emphasize that practitioners can begin with small steps using existing infrastructure, then build dedicated systemic investing solutions over time.

We present three practitioner profiles that exemplify the journey of innovators in the space, showing how they work across asset classes in strategic and integrated ways.

Systemic investing requires deep cross-sectoral collaboration. In practice, this means adopting a portfolio-level approach so as to incorporate different stakeholder perspectives and synergize across asset classes.

This field is evolving rapidly, and there is much scope for collaboration with diverse stakeholders, including fellow private investors, academia, public funders, or field builders.

I N TR ODUCT ION

What is systemic investing? Systemic investing is an emerging approach to capital deployment at the nexus of impact investing, philanthropy, and sustainable finance. These current approaches do not usually take a systemic perspective, focusing instead on individual point solutions (e.g. replacing internal combustion engines with electric motors) and ignoring the interconnected nature underpinning these challenges (e.g. outdated personal transportation systems). The resulting portfolios often lack synergy or, worse, contain investments that counteract each other. The growing community engaged in systemic investing believes that we must face humanity’s most pressing challenges in a collaborative and holistic manner. This mindset recognizes that social and ecological issues cannot 9

be addressed in isolation, due to the deeply interconnected nature of the systems that generate them. Systemic investing seeks to better understand the complexity of these systems and to create value through portfolios of synergistic investments, in coordination with other investors and stakeholders. Systems thinking is a set of concepts that now permeates much of modern culture. The use of terminology such as “tipping points”, “feedback loops”, and “mental models” often tends to be implicit and intuitively understood. In the investment world, systemic investors are now introducing these concepts intentionally and explicitly. We refer to this explicit introduction and use of systems thinking as a systems turn, with systemic investing being one manifestation that is reshaping capital deployment.

Background

We interpret systemic investing as primarily evolving through the introduction of systems thinking into impact investing. Both seek to advance ecological sustainability and human well-being, though targeting concrete improvements directly is not what defines systemic investing. Investing to directly generate eco-social outcomes, or “point-solution investing”, is the purview of impact investing. Systemic investing shifts the focal point away from direct outcome targeting, and places it on catalyzing changes in the systems generating those outcomes. If we take the example of the food system, then some of the problems to be addressed include emissions, resource-use intensity, food insecurity, and human rights violations. In impact investing, actors will use the tools available to them, e.g. VC capital or infrastructure funding, and make investments to address one of the problems, e.g. methane-capture tech for cattle. Looking at the problem systemically, however, research from the TransCap Initiative found that two of the most critical issues to address in the US food system are capacity-building for farmers and new insurance products. While somewhat oversimplistic, the differentiation is often summarized in the assertion that “traditional” impact investing sees the world as linear in nature, seeking to improve distinct metrics. Systemic investing sees the

world as a set of complex and interrelated systems, which it seeks to transform. Table 1 introduces a set of contrasts to illustrate this difference. Impact investing uses single asset classes to support point solutions to specific problems. Systemic investing uses multiple asset classes simultaneously to recalibrate the underlying system generating the problem. The shift in focus from addressing individual issues to meeting the needs of the system leads to very different solutions. This, in turn, leads to changes in the resources used, the understanding of portfolio construction, and the nature of stakeholder knowledge required.

Adding value through systemic investing

In an increasingly uncertain world, systemic investing offers a route to sustainably adding financial and eco-social value. This value is derived from embracing and utilizing the complexity of systems. Two mechanisms that can provide systemic investors with an edge are leverage points and synergistic investments. In the context of systemic investing, leverage refers to using one’s understanding of a system to identify the most effective points to intervene. “Leverage points” are thus where a targeted investment can catalyze the greatest change in the calibration of the system. This is also referred to as having a “trim tab” effect, where a small investment of resources can create outsized effects.

Having a comprehensive (and accurate) understanding of a system enables highly targeted capital deployment, leading to greater value. The capacity to identify leverage points in a system opens up the possibility of investing at multiple points in a synergistic manner. For example, producing an appealing electric car will not move the needle without simultaneous deployment of charging stations. Systemic investing therefore deploys capital to ensembles of solutions and their enabling conditions to explicitly generate these synergies. This requires investing across asset classes—including philanthropy and other forms of capital. Identifying and realizing synergies across

multi-asset portfolios is therefore a key characteristic of systemic investing. The use of such “strategic portfolios” to create value through synergies is a different way to think about diversification, moving beyond its use to manage risk in traditional portfolio construction. So how do we move from the big picture to actionable steps? To help contextualize and better digest systemic investing, the following sections feature four key insights.

“There were, and are, many investors in the alternative protein space with good intentions of helping reduce animal-based meat consumption and reducing strain on agriculture and land in order to improve the planet. But it’s critical to move past the mentality of thinking that investing in singular enterprises will move the needle. After our predecessor fund Closed Loop Capital invested in Beyond Meat, we realized we also needed to invest vertically in companies that were upstream in the food supply chain. To maximize impact, we need to see the fuller picture and identify opportunities for our portfolio companies to reinforce each other. And ideally, we need to look even beyond just the food sector and look at other interconnected horizontal systems.” Jason Ingle — Founder and Managing Partner, Third Nature Investments

INSIGHT 2

System boundaries are arbitrary but necessary

When we take on the mindset shift of systems thinking, a common tendency is to see everything as interconnected. Challenges of food insecurity, chronic disease, climate change, inequality, corruption, short termism, conflict, crime, urban sprawl, and biodiversity loss all influence each other, and they share common root causes in human psychology and (financial) incentives. The issues we face in a specific community link out to global trade, supply chains, and climate change. It can appear that we must address “everything everywhere all at once” to solve anything. 19

But investing is a practical activity; it involves making choices as we allocate capital and build portfolios. Managing the tension between a holistic perspective and pragmatic action requires the systemic investor to draw system boundaries, which are arbitrary borders around the space in which they work. System boundaries create limits to complexity and a defined space for action. These borders are provisional; they may expand or contract as system understanding deepens and collaboration brings new perspectives to the table.

In the first empirical study of systemic investing, MIT researcher Alban Yau noted that investors with an intention for systems change would draw their boundaries in three dimensions:

1. Geographic: Is the effort a place-based effort within a particular community or bioregion? Does it span to a national/ regional scope? Or does it seek global reach and impact? 2. Getting to a workable system boundary is not easy. It involves careful reflection on one’s purpose and vision, as well as understanding the realities of the system itself. Some geographies, issues, and sectors may feel “close to home”—more familiar, understandable, and emotionally resonant to investors and their stakeholders. Others may feel further afield, for example in frontier markets, but may have greater opportunities for impact.

The tools under development for systemic investing look at systems with multiple lenses: what problems are worth solving; where our capital can have greatest impact; what makes us come alive; or what can yield more resources, knowledge, relationships, and reputation that enable the work to continue.

Phases in understanding a system Source: Jason Jay, MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative

Given the complexity inherent within systems, it should come as no surprise that understanding them is not always straightforward. While we are strong proponents of the“just get started”tactic, comprehensively understanding a system is as essential as it is demanding. Here is a diagram that illustrates the phases of system understanding. 23

The process starts at the point of formulating what you need to understand and “spewing” all elements that you think are relevant. Nobody will ever have all the answers, so this step is about identifying your knowledge gaps. Equipped with a solid grasp of your ignorance, the journey toward better understanding can begin in earnest. The cycles go through gathering new stakeholders and new information, then synthesis and validation, and onto testing the accuracy of your understanding in practice.

The interaction with reality invariably sheds light on blind spots, and the cycle starts anew. While a basic iteration can be done alone, it is crucial to expand the number of stakeholders involved as you repeat the cycle to build a comprehensive picture.

This iterative process can be used to create a system map, which visually depicts the connections between various elements of a system. These elements could include the stakeholders and their relationships, or investments and the outcomes they generate. There are a number of different formats to map a system. One useful approach is based on “reinforcing loops” and “balancing loops” that drive changes in key “stocks and flows” of the system. Drawing on John Sterman’s seminal work on systems dynamics, we use the fishing 24

industry as an example above. In this first diagram, we can see that the catch initially increases due to investment in more boats and tech. Reinforcing loops More investment into tech and boats will increase revenues, and thus spur more investment. This positive relationship between the elements is thus called a reinforcing loop. Balancing loops However, fish are not infinite, so eventually the catch will begin to drop. The broken

orange line depicts a negative relationship, where an increase in catch leads to a decrease in fish, and vice versa. When a single negative relationship is present, then that part of the system will act as a balancing loop. Of course, there are many factors that influence this dynamic. To illustrate, we introduce more relevant factors in an expanded systems map on the following page.

Logically, the total catch is influenced by the catch per ship and the size of the fleet. Looking first at the right hand loop, we can see that the fish stocks play a central role in influencing the catch per ship. But what influences the size of the fleet? The loop on the left demonstrates that the fleet expands as investment increases the number of boats, assuming that the business is profitable. For profitability, the price of fish plays a key role. When profitability is high, more investment is made, fleets expand, and total catch increases.

But at some point the fish stocks are exhausted. When that happens, the revenues are not sufficient to cover the operating costs, as depicted by the negative relationship in the smaller lefthand loop. With lower profit comes lower investment, a shrinking fleet, and lower total catch. Thus the loop with operating costs acts as a balancing loop.

INSIGHT 4

Getting started involves fundamental shifts in practice

As discussed in Insight 1, a mindset shift is a significant first step and can be a powerful development, but insights 2 and 3 demonstrate it takes concerted effort to make a real difference in the world. We now look at two considerations for getting started in systemic investing.

Deep cross-sectoral collaboration One of the biggest adjustments to beginning in systemic investing is its fundamentally collaborative nature. The obvious reason for this is that as systems are complex, no one actor can see the whole system, and the variety of interests make it challenging to define success. As a result, the processes involved in transforming systems need input and collaborative effort from a range of stakeholders. Looking again at the example of the fishing industry, there needs to be input from representatives of as many of the relevant stakeholder groups as possible: fishing communities, NGOs, academics, policy experts, investors, etc. That input is used to synthesize an understanding of how a system currently operates and how it should operate in the future. Ideally, the end product will be representative of the views of all constituents of the system. If input is lacking from key stakeholders, then successful efforts to

change the configuration of a system in the short-term will not hold in the long-term. There must be collaboration proportionate to the scale and complexity of the system targeted. Later in this section we examine some practicalities of investing in a systemic manner, but the resources needed will be drawn from the systems’ constituents. Different actors bring different resources, and it is only through the synergistic deployment of those resources that a sustainable shift in a system can occur. To transform the fishing industry, this might include obvious resources such as funding from investors or public bodies, but the expertise and networks of NGOs or community groups will be just as significant. Catalyzing sustainable shifts in the dynamics of a system is thus an inherently collaborative process. Open and honest exchanges are vital to building a shared understanding of the needs of the system, and success is more likely when actively sharing the decision-making power on how resources are to be allocated.

A portfolio perspective to synergize across asset classes The defining characteristic in systemic investing practice is the shift in focus from single assets to synergies across asset classes. Given the diversity of assets, a portfolio-level perspective is essential to ensure that potential value gets realized. But what does that mean in practice? After a system is mapped, the investment requirements can be assessed.

Once these requirements have been estimated, a funding plan can be formulated for the systemic intervention. The plan can incorporate a range of capital sources, including commercial investments, concessional capital, or philanthropic funding. These capital sources are bundled to enable different actors to engage and to target specific points in the system. Figure 7 shows how various forms of capital can be configured for a systemic investing program.

It is important to note that systemic investing can make use of an array of resources. While we have focused on the deployment of economic capital, there are other forms of capital, such as social or cultural capital, that can also be deployed as part of a systemic investing strategy. These strategies are explored in greater detail in CSP’s forthcoming Investor’s Guide to Multicapital Strategies.

Image: Annual training program by Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth and MIT Sloan Sustainability: ‘’Investing for Systems Change’. Oslo, Norway, May 26-28, 2024

Notably, philanthropic funding often plays a catalytic role for enabling factors in a systemic investing program, particularly in the early stages. Returnseeking investment can be structured using strategic portfolios that comprise a variety of asset classes, ensuring that the intervention has an array of tools available.The interplay between the various capital deployments should generate added value due to the synergies. Seeking to add value through synergies across asset classes is a major departure from the traditional risk paradigm in the investment world, shifting the focus from risk-return to synergies-return optimization. It can take time to embed this logic within an organization and requires commitment to sustain.

Systemic investing programs have several practical ramifications that diverge significantly from standard investment paradigms: 1. Working across asset classes in strategic and integrated ways 2. Moving the unit of analysis from the single asset to the level of the portfolio 3. Changing the portfolio paradigm from risk reduction to value amplification 4. Collaborating deeply with other stakeholders, including foundations, governments 5. Reconceptualizing risk, returns and impact through a systemic lens The previous sections detailed the background and the theoretical underpinnings of systemic investing. We have seen how systems thinking is permeating the investing world, what such a mindset entails and the practical implications. In the next section we will explore how those elements come together in practice.

Practitioner profiles Systemic investing involves the synergistic deployment of capital for systems transformation. The ways to engage can encompass a diverse toolkit such as commercial investments, catalytic investments, and philanthropy. The profiles in this section feature a variety of approaches and starting points in practitioners’ journeys.

We can only provide static representations, which become dated very quickly. Given that our objective is to provide an actionable guide, the profiles should be understood as points of orientation for those interested in beginning their own systemic investing journey.

The vignettes below are designed to introduce steps for getting started in systemic investing. There are four parts to each profile, though it is crucial to note that they are neither sequential nor static, given that the activities necessary to successfully engage in systemic investing are continuously evolving. 1. Scoping the problem space: Each profile provides a table that captures the geographic and sectoral boundaries they set for their activities. We also touch on the strategy employed to achieve their objectives. These components need to be examined together as the objectives set out through the strategy need to be aligned with the resources available. 2. Understanding the system: Drawing on the framework introduced above, each profile also contains details on key characteristics of the target system. This helps to articulate the systems understanding that the systemic investor has built out. As noted above, it is essential to engage with others to establish a holistic picture over time. 3. Tracking the journey: We use a timeline format to illustrate the key steps taken by the practitioners and how their roles have adapted over time. The timelines begin with key moments experienced by the founders, small steps taken through existing infrastructure, and later building into dedicated systemic investing solutions. 4. Establish the systemic investing practice: We include descriptions of investments made to illustrate how the practitioners have sought to generate synergies through resource deployment in different asset classes. The descriptions include a note on the type of investment and the leverage point targeted. These profiles capture the paths taken by some of the pioneers in this field. Despite their diverse starting points, there are signs of convergence in their practice. The growing polycrisis faced by humanity is sharpening their focus and fueling a desire to think and act as holistically and collaboratively as possible.

Tara Health Foundation The Tara Health Foundation, established in 2014, exemplifies an evolution towards systemic investing in the philanthropic sector. With an initial focus on improving the health and wellbeing of women and girls within a 20-year time frame, the foundation evolved to actively advance racial equity, racial justice, and gender justice as deeply intertwined pillars of its mission. Tara Health’s commitment to aligning 100% of its assets with its mission through the creative use of philanthropic capital demonstrates the systemic nature of its approach to investing. The foundation aims to spend down the entirety of its assets by 2030, ensuring lasting impact through recalibrating the health system to better serve the intersection of race and gender.

Tara Health Foundation Timeline 1990 Dr. Ruth Shaber begins her career as an Obstetrician Gynecologist. In addition to her clinical career, she held multiple leadership positions in evidence-based practices and systems approaches to create reliable clinical performance across large health care systems.

2014 Tara Health Foundation is established with an initial endowment of $80M, drawing on Dr. Shaber’s experience in health care systems and evidence-based practice.

2016 Tara Health creatively leverages its philanthropic capital to support critical abortion providers, offering a blend of low-interest debt and unrestricted grant dollars. Begins showcasing the use of innovative philanthropic capital to support abortion care while strengthening the broader reproductive health ecosystem.

2017 Moves towards becoming a blended capital institution; convenes the Reproductive Health Investors Alliance, bringing together key foundations and investors to determine evidence-based opportunities for investment in the reproductive health space.

2020 Allocates additional funding to its grantmaking budget for a rapid response grantmaking strategy during the COVID-19 pandemic and the Movement for Black Lives, shortening the foundation’s spenddown timeline by five years.

2021 Finalizes its strategy for spendingdown, committing 100% of its assets to organizations and leaders working at the intersection of race and gender, transferring power and resources to those most affected by and equipped to address these systemic issues.

2022 Begin the process of transferring all resources and assets, marking the start of the spend-down strategy.

2023 Research findings show VC capital flows into women’s health up 314% from 2018 levels, implying systemic impact of Tara Health’s and others’ investments.

2028 – 2030 Projected completion of the process to transfer all resources and assets.

The Good Investors The Good Investors (TGI) is a collective of families with a mission to transform essential systems such as food, water, energy, and biodiversity through systemic investing. TGI aims to drive sustainable change by supporting early to growth-stage actors, both financially and through stakeholder engagement, with the potential to trigger broad transformative effects. While the initial impulse to engage systemically can be traced back to 2009 when one of TGI’s founding families started focusing on sustainable and impact investing, TGI’s systemic investing strategy is built on establishing a portfolio capable of both transforming systems and generating returns superior to“traditional” VC / private equity investment. TGI leverages strategic partnerships and systemic perspectives to achieve this financial performance while addressing complex global challenges. Conscious of the need for rapid development of a viable ecosystem, TGI also engages significant human and financial resources to help build the field of systemic investing through research and collaboration. How to put this guide into action

Systems are complex, but getting started in systemic investing need not be. When working in, or on, systems, interacting with one part will have effects across the interrelated components. Knowing this can lead to analysis paralysis and a perception that engaging in systemic investing might be an unavoidably complex undertaking. However, there are accessible paths to begin the journey. Looking at the steps that are characteristic of current systemic investing processes, we have highlighted some that are feasible with varying investment of time and capital. 47

How to put this guide into action

Scoping your problem space

Depending on your level of ambition and the resources available, start by identifying that part of a system you could feasibly hope to influence. This usually involves focusing on a sector like apparel or tourism, an issue like climate change or opportunity gaps, and a geographic area such as a city, country, or region. Can you articulate some changes you would like to see in the configuration of that system? To catalyze change, you will need to deal with ambiguity, you will need to immerse yourself, and there will be a great deal of iteration and learning-by-doing. It will take time, and there are no shortcuts, no easy answers. You will be challenged by others, and you will need to challenge yourself in a process of selfunderstanding and inner development. Focusing on a topic that is of genuine interest is crucial as it will help ensure that you stay motivated and engaged as you move forward.

Reflection questions ⁕ What is the single most important topic for you? ⁕ Why is this important to you? If you took a systemic investing approach to address it, what system would you be most interested in working on? ⁕ What issues or problems would you aim to solve? What geographic area would be feasible to address? ⁕ What assets do you currently employ in your (impact) investing, and is there overlap with your target system? 48

Understanding the system

Having scoped a problem space, you will need to deepen your understanding of that system. We have highlighted how to “access your ignorance” by sketching out your initial understanding of the system. Try this process yourself, investing as much or as little time as you like. This initial work provides a basis for assessing your ideas for a healthier configuration of the system, perhaps mapping potential leverage points or areas of synergies. Understanding the system is a crucial activity that needs to be constantly revisited, also with other stakeholders. This iterative process helps to understand your position and to identify areas of overlap between your interests and the resource base you can mobilize. These parameters will shape your strategy as you begin to engage, and they help immediately when assessing your role and finding potential collaborators.

Consider your role

As part of understanding the system, you will be constantly mapping the relevant actors and initiating contact with key stakeholders. You can look to fellow wealth holders, businesses, local community leaders, NGOs, think tanks, public administrators, academics, and elsewhere. There is also a growing ecosystem of investor groups and service providers engaging around systemic investing (we provide an initial list below). This discovery phase is crucial for a range of reasons: avoiding duplication, establishing a holistic understanding of the system, identifying points for intervention, finding allies, and more. It is almost certain that others are seeking to address the same issue that you are looking at. As you move forward, you can collaborate to establish shared understanding and inclusive governance structures for decision-making.

Reflection questions ⁕ What role do I want to play? ⁕ What capitals do I bring to bear—e.g. financial, reputational, network, or knowledge—that can maximize my effectiveness in that role? ⁕ Who do I currently collaborate with? ⁕ Who else could I collaborate with given the scale and complexity of my target system?

At times your access to certain resources may be more limited, while at other times you enjoy greater autonomy. Either way, the processes elaborated in this guide help identify points where you can intervene in a target system and begin your systemic investing practice. Some initial starting points might include: a. Support a “backbone” organization: Backbone organizations are the players in a space that help to bring together actors and orchestrate efforts to effect change. These are often nonprofit entities established exactly for this purpose and providing them with support (e.g. financial, network, time) is an excellent way to gain understanding of and knowledge about a system. b. Make synergy-seeking investments: To build up systemic investing capacity over time, look to make philanthropic and financial investments that are synergistic with your existing investments. This could involve providing an R&D grant for a new tech solution, investing up- or downstream to ensure that solution has suppliers and customers, or founding a new backbone organization (if none exists). Starting small and iterating is the best way to drive learnings on how and where new investments should be placed to create synergies with existing one(s). c. Bring in the pros: While not yet a widely established practice, there are a number of systemic investing advisory firms emerging. Working with a specialized advisor can greatly accelerate the process of strategy development and deployment. There are also training programs, such as the Investing for Systems Change program run annually by the Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth (CSP) in collaboration with the MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative that can help investors begin their systemic investing journey. It may also be possible to join with an existing investor group that is addressing the system you want to target.

At times your access to certain resources may be more limited, while at other times you enjoy greater autonomy. Either way, the processes elaborated in this guide help identify points where you can intervene in a target system and begin your systemic investing practice. Some initial starting points might include: a. Support a “backbone” organization: Backbone organizations are the players in a space that help to bring together actors and orchestrate efforts to effect change. These are often nonprofit entities established exactly for this purpose and providing them with support (e.g. financial, network, time) is an excellent way to gain understanding of and knowledge about a system. b. Make synergy-seeking investments: To build up systemic investing capacity over time, look to make philanthropic and financial investments that are synergistic with your existing investments. This could involve providing an R&D grant for a new tech solution, investing up- or downstream to ensure that solution has suppliers and customers, or founding a new backbone organization (if none exists). Starting small and iterating is the best way to drive learnings on how and where new investments should be placed to create synergies with existing one(s). c. Bring in the pros: While not yet a widely established practice, there are a number of systemic investing advisory firms emerging. Working with a specialized advisor can greatly accelerate the process of strategy development and deployment. There are also training programs, such as the Investing for Systems Change program run annually by the Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth (CSP) in collaboration with the MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative that can help investors begin their systemic investing journey. It may also be possible to join with an existing investor group that is addressing the system you want to target.

Engaging with potential collaborators We produced this guide to provide wealth holders with a first touchpoint to the nascent field of systemic investing. We are very aware that there are other actors with whom collaboration is essential for systemic investing. With that in mind, we provide some final thoughts for wealth holders on how to engage with these stakeholder groups.

FE LLOW W E A L T H H O L D E R S

Be open and intentional Given the multitude of issues humanity is facing, many wealth holders feel a growing burden of responsibility to invest their resources in a useful way. Some also feel constrained by their familial or organizational context, but the most important point is to find collaborators and a sense of community. A commonly used proverb by practitioners in this space is: “If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.” Reaching out to fellow wealth holders, helping them reflect on their personal journey, building out syndication and deal-sharing capacity, or inviting them to join communities of practice are ways to expand the network of wealth holders engaged in systemic investing. It is only through networks that sufficient resources can be mobilized to effectively structure strategic portfolios.

W E A L T H M A NA G E R S A ND F I NA NC I A L S E R VI C E P R O VID ERS

The past will not be as useful in the future Investments will need to become increasingly sophisticated vis-à-vis understanding systems to maintain financial performance moving forward. In the face of the geopolitical instability caused by accelerated technological evolution and the climate/nature crises, there will be a large drop in the utility of past performance data from management teams, asset classes, verticals, and others. Systemic investing is about being able to map and model systems in order to invest in, and for, their health and stability. It is not an easy task, but maintaining financial performance will involve working with those wealth managers and service providers who can generate synergies across multiasset portfolios and contribute to healthy systems for all.

R ESEARC HE RS

PUB LI C F U ND E R S

FIELD BUILDERS

Learning how to manage complexity

Potential for greater coordination in resource allocation

Managing tensions to unlock potential

There are myriad topics that could be researched in the nascent field of systemic investing. Some of these are more practical, others more theoretical. As part of your systemic investing activity, you could directly support research organizations who are examining or mapping a specific system. Alternatively, you could provide fieldbuilding support for systemic investing by funding academics researching the significance of backbone organizations for systemic transformation. As with other systems, the knowledge system is so interconnected that advances made in “practical” and “theoretical” areas of research will produce synergies. Where you choose to engage is less relevant than maintaining ties with researchers. This is good practice as researchers provide an external perspective that is particularly relevant where resource allocation is involved, given the power dynamics in play when choosing systems to target and formulating desired futures.

There is rapidly building pressure on public budgets to address national and international development issues. Systemic investing holds the potential to act as a bridging conceptual framework for greater efficacy when coordinating your investment activity with public funders. To date, efforts at coordinated investment have largely involved infrastructure Public and Private Partnerships. While useful, that approach is extremely limited and can only provide appropriate finance for a small subset of the efforts that need to be supported. Systemic investing can facilitate the development and articulation of shared objectives, and act to coherently blend private assets and public funding. If you are looking to collaborate with public funders, some areas to investigate would include R&D, innovation, entrepreneurship, international development, community finance, or climate adaptation.

Building a field requires both a bringing together of diverse actors and a reconfiguration of the relations between those actors. The ability to manage tensions is thus a key determinant of a field builder’s success. In systemic investing, there is presently a tension between the need for methodological and conceptual rigor, and ensuring accessibility to the field. There are thus different ways to support field builders in their efforts to produce more differentiated communication materials. This can mean ensuring that there is an on-ramp for newcomers or pushing forward with pioneers looking to build increasingly sophisticated theory and practice. There is also work to be done on both building understanding within specific communities of resource allocators (public or private), and the need to build bridges between these communities. The former is often an easier starting point, but the latter holds greater potential for systemic transformation.

MIT Sloan Research Paper No. 6596-23, 2023. ⮑ This case study examines how systemic investing was applied to address food waste in the U.S., showcasing the strategic use of different forms of capital to drive systemic change in the food system. Meadows, Donella. Thinking in Systems: A Primer. (Re)Calibrating Feedback Loops. Investor’s Guide to Multicapital Strategies

Foreword

Dr. Falko Paetzold Founder, CSP; Managing Director, CCSP-HSG Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth

Dr. Jason Jay Senior Lecturer and Director MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative

Seth Fleisher Managing Director, Americas Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth

Renee Kaplan Chief Executive Officer Forward Global

David P Dietz Director of Impact NEXUS

Over the last decade, we have engaged with many impact-focused wealth holders who share a key concern: their desire to create meaningful change exceeds what their current financial position enables. Many inheritors find themselves eager to deploy capital for impact but must wait while older generations, prioritizing traditional financial returns, maintain control over investment decisions. Similarly, entrepreneurs often feel limited while their funds are still tied up in a business. Even those with complete control of their assets often feel these are insufficient against the scale of today's global challenges, leaving them seeking additional ways to amplify their impact. What do all these wealth holders have in common? They think of their resources purely as economic, thereby dramatically underestimating the power of their social capital (networks), symbolic capital (reputation) and cultural capital (skills and knowledge). But everyone, especially wealth holders, has a range of capitals at their disposal.

This guide offers a deep dive into the capital types, how each is uniquely positioned to facilitate impact and the inherent power in their combination. This foundation allows for strategic alignment in service of the impact wealth holders want to create in the world. As always, this strategy requires thoughtful consideration of wealth holders’ influence, ensuring that power—in whatever form it takes—is exercised responsibly for the greater good. The Insights in this guide are informed by 27 leading impact-focused wealth holders we interviewed to understand their capital allocations. We triangulated these findings with academic and applied literature, ultimately answering the question: How have impact-driven wealth holders deployed their capitals for good, and what can we learn from these practices? This is their story—and a roadmap for your own multicapital journey. Let’s get started—toward impact!

About this guide At the Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth (CSP), University of St.Gallen (CCSP-HSG), NEXUS, Forward Global and the MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative, we recognize that wealth holders’ capacity to positively impact the world begins with a deep understanding of their resources, which are far more than just economic. We draw on academic theory, insights from practice, and primary research. Through 27 in-depth interviews with experienced investors from Europe, North America, Asia and Australia, we explored how deeply engaged investors and philanthropists strategize the use of their economic and noneconomic resources. Interviewees highlighted the critical role of relationships, reputations, and knowledge

in driving impact alongside, or even in the absence of, economic capital. These rich conversations inform our key insights and framework, demonstrating how resource flows can accelerate (or decelerate) impact. This guide aims to equip current and future wealth holders with actionable approaches to amplify the positive environmental and social impact they have in the world. It also emphasizes that ethical approaches to deploying influence require transparency in decisionmaking, the incorporation of complementary voices and accountability for actions—principles that become even more crucial as wealth holders activate diverse forms of capital.

Executive summary This guide reveals how wealth holders can harness their potential for positive change by strategically deploying all their resources— not just money, but relationships, knowledge, and reputation as well. Multicapital strategies demonstrate how impact emerges when these diverse capitals work in combination.

Four types of capital Traditional investing and philanthropy focus solely on economic resources, leaving other valuable assets untapped. Strategic impact requires understanding and deploying four distinct capital types:

Economic capital

Social capital

Cultural capital

Symbolic capital

Money and assets that grant access to people and spaces— while creating opportunities to catalyze change and generate learning.

Relationships that activate communities, foster trust, and facilitate influence within groups.

Knowledge and skills that can challenge existing social norms and empower others.

Reputation that attracts attention and acts as a multiplier, amplifying or converting other forms of capital.

I NTRO D UC TIO N

Jeff's story Disrupting discriminatory housing practices

During a fellowship at the Aspen Institute, Jeff deepened his understanding of how discriminatory housing practices have prevented Black families in the United States from building generational wealth, creating cascading disadvantages that persist across generations. For Jeff, this knowledge came with a moral imperative. After selling New Leaf Paper, a leading sustainable paper company and a founding Benefit Corporation, Jeff faced a crossroads. He could have pursued any number of ventures, continuing his entrepreneurial success. Instead, he decided to co-found LocalCode, a nonprofit organization which builds wealth through local ownership of real estate in low-income communities. Jeff launched LocalCode in Kansas City, supporting local, Black female entrepreneurs in regenerative real estate development that builds wealth and wellbeing in their communities. Over the past five years, LocalCode has helped its Kansas City affiliates establish a $250 million pipeline, directly countering extractive development patterns that have historically harmed communities of color. Jeff's initial investment, experience as an entrepreneur and network of relationships with real estate developers have proven instrumental in establishing the business model and securing funding, while the local entrepreneurs he supports 11

have deep community roots, ensuring that the properties they develop truly serve residents' needs. Moreover, the impact extends beyond individual properties. LocalCode is demonstrating a replicable model for how communities can reclaim control over their economic development and address the root causes of race-based economic inequality. Jeff’s approach offers a blueprint for how wealth holders can meaningfully contribute to addressing systemic inequities while ensuring those most affected retain agency over the solutions.

More than money: all the resources enabling impact Jeff’s investment in LocalCode is a key part of his story. In fact, it would be the central focus of the narrative if this was another publication about impact investing. But the economic capital invested is clearly not the most impactful part of Jeff’s story. His investment was only possible because of his other resources—his relationships, skills, experience and reputation. What’s more, Jeff is not unique. All the wealth holders we interviewed told stories of the values and resources that inspire their impact in the world. Isolating economic capital in impact strategies is choosing to understand only one fraction of reality. Considering capital as purely economic treats the many other resources that enable and complement economic capital as immaterial, when they have always been essential.

LocalCode is demonstrating a replicable model for how communities can reclaim control over their economic development and address the root causes of race-based economic inequality. Jeff’s approach offers a blueprint for how wealth holders can meaningfully contribute to addressing systemic inequities while ensuring those most affected retain agency over the solutions.

More than money: all the resources enabling impact Jeff’s investment in LocalCode is a key part of his story. In fact, it would be the central focus of the narrative if this was another publication about impact investing. But the economic capital invested is clearly not the most impactful part of Jeff’s story. His investment was only possible because of his other resources—his relationships, skills, experience and reputation. What’s more, Jeff is not unique. All the wealth holders we interviewed told stories of the values and resources that inspire their impact in the world. Isolating economic capital in impact strategies is choosing to understand only one fraction of reality. Considering capital as purely economic treats the many other resources that enable and complement economic capital as immaterial, when they have always been essential.

Defining capital and the types of capital

Scholars and practitioners alike have grappled for more than 150 years with how to make sense of the term“capital”. This guide combines and distills the wisdom of a deep body of literature with the lived experience of leading impact investors deploying capital in the real world. The result is a clear and actionable approach for wealth holders wanting to mobilize all their resources for impact. In particular, we emphasize how you can deliberately deploy your network of relationships, knowledge and experience, and reputation alongside your financial resources—often with multiplier effects.

All accumulated, deployable resources an individual can mobilize to generate value within specific systems. This definition is rigorous yet practical, and will help you to: ⁕ See your resources in a new light:

capitals in context, at specific points in time, to amplify the impact you have with your resources.

your capitals: Consider how each capital's investment sets you up for greater positive impact in the future.

Capital in theory and practice In the field of academic inquiry, the idea of capital as more than money has a long history. Starting with the association of capital with people’s labor in Das Kapital by Karl Marx in 18671, to more recent and broad definitions of capital, such as Bourdieu’s framework, which categorizes capital as economic, social, cultural or symbolic in nature2, scholars define capital in many ways beyond money. For example, Robert Putnam3, Mark Granovetter4 and others focus on the quality, quantity and structure of relationships that comprise social capital, while Michele Lamont and others address the knowledge and experiences that take the form of cultural capital5. Still others discuss forms including human6, natural7 and spiritual capital8. The academic discussion of capital is useful in its ability to define and differentiate. The field of practice also grapples with how to categorize and think about our multiple resources. The philanthropic field talks about using one’s “time, talent and ties” in addition to one’s “treasure.” Others have developed language and concepts to address inherent strength in the plurality of these resources, discussing poly-capitalism9 or polycapital10, in reference to the multiple types of capital that can be leveraged toward positive impact. Still others have imagined the capability of these resources as enabling the transformation of capitalism itself, from our current “monocapitalism” to a more humane and sustainable “multicapitalism.” 11 The widely-ranging discussion of capitals in both academic and practice-based discussions suggests that the term has become a catchall for any type of resource and, by extension, lost much of its use-value. This guide condenses insights from these ongoing discussions, narrowing the definition of capital to the wealth that an individual can leverage.

Foundational concepts of capital

FOUN D A TION A L C O N C E P T 1

Four types of capital For this guide’s purpose—to help wealth holders simplify, define and mobilize their resources for impact—we categorize all resources as pertaining to one of four capital types2:

Economic capital

Social capital

Cultural capital

Symbolic capital

Money and nonmonetary assets (like real estate or intellectual property), that can convert to money.

Relationships, including their types, numbers, and quality, i.e., trust.

Knowledge, from formal (e.g., professional trainings) and informal (e.g., childhood) experiences.

Reputation or prestige belonging to a person individually or as a representative of a group (e.g., name of family or business).

F O UN D A TION A L C O N C E P T 2

Core characteristics of capital Capital has three fundamental characteristics. Understanding these will help you to identify not only which ones you have, but also when and how you might use them.

Capital moves in healthy systems Central to our definition of capital is rethinking the assumption that money and other resources are “gone” after we spend or use them. Instead, we want to emphasize that capital moves; it should flow through systems and environments as individuals and organizations accumulate, hold and deploy it. Economic and social capital movement is often impeded by traditional wealth management, which retains capital in structures like legacy real estate and exclusive networks. When capital does not flow, it creates broader social challenges.

Capital’s value is relational12 Capital moves between two or more people and organizations, and the value of capital is inherently tied to this relationality. The relational nature of capital enables it to be accrued and deployed. For instance, economic capital can't be mobilized for affordable housing projects without developers and communities that want to partner and local officials who will approve permits to build.

Capital deployment depends on the right context 13 Economic capital can be moved between contexts, and global markets have made it easy to do so. By contrast, the deployability of noneconomic capitals (cultural, social and symbolic) varies greatly depending upon the context. Certain places or groups of people may value these capitals more than others. For example, if you are a famous movie star, you have lots of symbolic capital, but that does not mean you can use it to get experienced investors to back your untested business idea. Why? While your fame might draw initial attention, the symbolic capital you possess as an entertainer does not directly translate to credibility in the business world. Similarly, having a famous family name or being known for starting a specific business might be of great value only in a specific region or to a specific audience.

F OUN D A TION A L C O N C E P T 3

Multicapital strategies can increase impact Combining the different types of capital creates opportunities for outsized impact relative to using only economic capital alone; possibly even in a multiplicative way. Findings from our interviews provide insightful examples of these combinations. Exploring a multicapital approach can help you to understand your capitals deeply, the relationships of capitals to one another, and how to strategize them for deployment.

Leveraging your unique capital portfolio

As the foundational concepts above demonstrate, each person has a unique set of capitals. As a wealth holder, you may have more capital to deploy than others, including some you may not be aware of yet. For instance, you might have an elite education, inherited or earned financial wealth, a famous last name, access to certain networks and more. And you may have already deployed and multiplied certain forms of capital, for instance, by investing economic capital to attain access to specific communities, or earning a reputation and making key relationships through a successful business endeavor. Defining these capitals and their relational nature makes them visible, which is the first step in understanding how to combine them strategically for impact.

Insights from practice

IN S IGHT 1

Values and early life experiences inform capital strategy The language of values or spirituality is not often present in discussions of money, but according to our interviewees, it should be—early and often. Whether referring to their values, spirituality, religion, kuleana, chokmah, consciousness or the sacred (all of which were mentioned), interviewees openly discussed the fundamental, shared understanding of life that informs not only their passions but the way they strategize and invest their resources. While values are not a deployable resource in the way other capitals are, they function as a lens through which people understand and deploy their resources. Alexa’s vision for the future inspires her investments and relationships

Alex’s inspiration sparked by sustainable business

Urs’ public commitment to giving back

Alexa Firmenich, advisor to SEED and founder, Naia Trust:

Dr. Alex Weisberg, Partner, Fieldston Group, connects his Jewish upbringing and education with the cultural capital he gained in university, where he says:

Urs Wietlisbach, Co-Founder, Partners Group and Blue Earth Capital.

“I

want to be surrounded by people that are deploying their resources because there's something deep in their hearts as to why this matters to them...I think only some of the things that are needed in the future will be very revenue generating, and a lot of the things that appear to be revenue generating are very much externalizing harm into other systems… the people I have had the delight of meeting are on a...high level journey.”

Alexa’s values inform her motivation to support a less harmful future. She uses her economic capital to invest, developing social capital alongside similarly motivated investors and cultural capital through her work with the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich (ETH Zurich) Crowther Lab, to support her vision.

“I

assumed school would not be a path towards environmental awareness, but then the CEO of Patagonia at the time came to talk to our group, and I was totally blown away by that. I had no idea that there were companies that were organized around ecological sustainability and social justice. And it sparked some sense of intuition in me.” Alex’s interest in the environment and focus on sustainability emerged from the connection between his family values and his formative educational experiences in school. He is one of several interviewees who connects his values and spiritual life to transformative experiences in school, living abroad, and early work experiences that either complemented or challenged these values.

Early in his career, Urs Wietlisbach was deeply influenced by Andrew Carnegie's "Gospel of Wealth"14. The book’s philosophy impressed upon him the responsibility of giving back to society after earning wealth. Along with other influences, Carnegie’s book shaped Urs’s decision to sign the Giving Pledge, committing publicly to contributing a majority of his wealth to philanthropy.

Alex Weisberg, PhD, Partner, Fieldston Power combined his Jewish background and doctoral degree with his learning about sustainable business from his MBA to improve and inspire his impact investing strategy.

Ruth Shaber, MD, Founder & President at Tara Health Foundation, gained formal education as a physician specializing in women's health and later developed expertise in financial systems through hands-on experience. Based on that she wrote a book, The XX Edge pairing her knowledge and experience with data to prove the financial advantage.

I NS IG HT 3

Combining capitals can accelerate or compromise impact Understanding the interplay of capitals can help you identify the best combination for a particular impact goal. While combining capitals often accelerates impact, there may be cases where your impact will be greater if you don’t deploy them all. We explore both examples in the section that follows.

Charly and Lisa Kleissner Toniic and Twist

Combining capitals can lead to more capital and new strategies

In general, capital can beget more capital. For instance, deploying economic capital may help an investor learn about effective impact strategies (building cultural capital), which can then be used to share a message (deploying symbolic capital), attract additional economic capital, and so on. In other words, leveraging one form of capital deliberately to acquire more of another form of capital may help you to better achieve your impact objectives. As Charly Kleissner explains of KL Felicitas Foundation’s investment in the first social impact bond, 26

“W

e made this investment hoping that thousands of impact bonds would be created, which could then be securitized into equities that would go up and down with proven positive or negative impact. This did not happen. But this experience informed our philanthropy and investment strategy as we explored the question: How can we do the next iteration of this intervention in a way that has the potential for more scale and broader success?”

Charly and Lisa Kleissner used innovative approaches to impact investing, which resulted in a range of impact outcomes. However, as Charly points out, deploying economic capital always led to a deeper understanding of impact, or the acquisition of cultural capital that shaped the next phase of their impact journey.

Withholding capital may serve impact priorities Deliberately withholding some capital you could deploy may allow you to gain credibility, center other communities, or achieve particular impact goals. Toni’s story Antonis Schwarz of Good Move Initiatives used inherited wealth to found the Guerrilla Foundation in 2016, which supports activists and grassroots movements working toward major systemic change across Europe. He continues to serve on the foundation’s “Funders Circle” and has recruited additional supporters through the foundation's internship program. As the seed donor, Toni initially had the right to decide the foundation's mission and grant recipients. However, 27

recognizing that others possessed greater expertise in activism and social movements, he worked with foundation staff and activist advisors to establish an Activist Council to award grants. This Council is now part of the foundation’s governance structure, ensuring that funding decisions are made by those best positioned to identify and support effective grassroots work, ultimately better achieving the impact objective. In 2023 alone, the Guerrilla Foundation made 76 grants totaling ca. €1 million in support of activists.

Raffi’s Multicapital strategy: A healthy Cambridge community Economic Capital

Social Capital

Created the opportunity to be catalytic, including supporting a newspaper and buying an apartment building to house refugees.

Trusting relationships with both policy makers and real estate developers, who are often not in alignment with one another.

Symbolic Capital Reputation as a knowledgeable and caring community member who supports philanthropically and politically and who is not in real estate development professionally.

Raffi’s story Raffi Freeman has a background in climate tech and sustainable development, having built a company in Rwanda to provide carbon-neutral power for the first mRNA vaccine production site in Africa. Following a successful exit in 2020, he shifted focus to community work in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Raffi Freeman Izuba Energy

During the 2021 evacuation of people from Afghanistan, he mobilized community support for refugee resettlement and purchased an apartment building to welcome newcomers. His local investment and volunteerism led him to a fundamental insight: to tackle climate change while ensuring

sufficient affordable housing, he needed to focus on a single critical issue—enabling housing density in Cambridge. His impactful engagements earned him a position on the city's Affordable Housing Trust Board. In this position, he is able to leverage relationships he has built with both real estate developers and city council members, aligning diverse stakeholders to achieve policy improvements. This impact was possible precisely because Raffi did not invest more broadly in real estate development, maintaining credibility as a knowledgeable and neutral partner.

Antonis Schwarz Good Move Initiatives

While Toni’s and Raffi’s stories are very different, both are marked by active decisions to combine capitals in strategic ways, as well as decisions to deliberately omit some of the capitals they might deploy. As Raffi’s example demonstrates, his decision not to invest alongside real estate developers in Cambridge was precisely what allowed him to broker relationships between the real estate developers he knew and policymakers. He centered the relationships, building trust that was not dependent upon his financial returns. This trust was critical to the sustainable housing policy changes he has successfully helped facilitate in Cambridge. Similarly, Toni’s decision to center activists’ knowledge about social change, as opposed to his own convictions, helps the Guerrilla Foundation’s mission and vision stay connected to the communities it exists to serve. While he could have leveraged his reputation as a founder to determine foundation grants, it would not serve his impact goal to empower activists. These examples demonstrate the thoughtful, agile and committed approach that multicapital strategies require of the wealth holders who undertake them, informing not only what capitals they combine but also those they intentionally do not deploy. 29

I NS IG HT 4

Systems awareness supports effective deployment The first three insights feature the role of the investor’s values, interests and capitals. The fourth considers broader systems. Understanding the system you want to impact is key to deploying multicapital strategies effectively. Our interviewees cite a number of ways that they incorporate their systems awareness.

Address root causes with creative approaches As Susan Weingartner, Owner and Strategic Advisor, Cambia Capital, explains, her focus on housing sits at the nexus of two crises— housing affordability and climate. While she acknowledges that housing may not be the market’s latest shiny object, she emphasizes its outsized impact.

“N

ew construction rarely gets the spotlight when it comes to sustainability. Everyone's chasing climate moonshots, and somehow housing doesn’t make the list. I don’t know why—it may not seem sexy, but I get to tell the stories that reveal just how critical it is.” Susan’s focus on housing didn’t stem from a childhood dream or a specific degree. It emerged from a deeper understanding of social inequality and environmental sustainability and the realization that housing can be a powerful lever for addressing both. With that conviction, she co-founded Green Canopy and later launched Cambia Capital to allocate investment capital into sustainable and accessible new construction, addressing the impact of housing on the climate and communities. Like Susan, Kelly Winget, Founder, Alternative Wealth Partners, leveraged investment to address a fundamental challenge in American society. Her focus on inadequate regulatory and enforcement

Adapt capital’s form and function mechanisms for gun safety led her to understand that market. In the United States, just a few, large companies have control over the supply chain in this market. So, she purchased a Texas business that produced the primer component for small-caliber ammunition. Although gun-related business seems far from an impact investment, Kelly used her ownership, purpose and deep sense of responsibility for private capital to radically re-strategize the business, keeping the change in American gun legislation she seeks front and center. She plans to leverage the company’s position in the American market to incentivize policies to reward responsible gun sales, safety features, ownership and education. Kelly’s investment demonstrates that a creative approach to ownership may enable innovative ways to address root causes at scale.

Ruth Shaber Tara Health Foundation

IN S IG HT 5

Multicapital deployment can also have systemic effects As the previous insight indicates, combining multiple capitals can help shift capital flows in systems. This means that multicapital strategies can also support systemic change.

Ruth Shaber, MD, founded Tara Health Foundation to transform reproductive health access and outcomes. She practiced medicine in obstetrics and gynecology for 25 years before establishing the Foundation. Ruth mobilized her knowledge about reproductive and broader women’s health alongside her philanthropic capital, influencing the marketplace in several ways. Through the Foundation, Ruth convened the Reproductive Health Investors Alliance (Rhia Ventures) in 2017, 32

garnering a network of values-aligned investors to boost capital flows into women’s health. She and Patience Marime-Ball also wrote the book, The XX Edge, Unlocking Higher Returns and Lower Risk, in 2022, which demonstrates the financial edge of including women as decision-makers in organizations. Ruth combined her knowledge as a physician, her network of peers and her philanthropy to catalyze a transformation in the field of women’s health. As of 2023, VC flows into women’s health were up 314%, suggesting that

Ruth’s and others’ investments have contributed to systemic shifts in funding for women’s health. Considering our global polycrisis, it is empowering to know that multicapital deployment is a potential tool for the broad systems change the world so urgently needs.

She practiced medicine in obstetrics and gynecology for 25 years before establishing the Foundation. Ruth mobilized her knowledge about reproductive and broader women’s health alongside her philanthropic capital, influencing the marketplace in several ways. Through the Foundation, Ruth convened the Reproductive Health Investors Alliance (Rhia Ventures) in 2017, 32

garnering a network of values-aligned investors to boost capital flows into women’s health. She and Patience Marime-Ball also wrote the book, The XX Edge, Unlocking Higher Returns and Lower Risk, in 2022, which demonstrates the financial edge of including women as decision-makers in organizations. Ruth combined her knowledge as a physician, her network of peers and her philanthropy to catalyze a transformation in the field of women’s health. As of 2023, VC flows into women’s health were up 314%, suggesting that

Ruth’s and others’ investments have contributed to systemic shifts in funding for women’s health. Considering our global polycrisis, it is empowering to know that multicapital deployment is a potential tool for the broad systems change the world so urgently needs.

Creating your capital inventory Before you can design an impact strategy, you need to know what capitals you have. While it is common practice to“know what you own”from an economic perspective, it is less common to think comprehensively about the relationships, knowledge or reputation you have and how they might be used to create positive change. The table opposite can help you identify the capitals you have and whether, how and when to allocate them toward impact.

S TE P 1

Identify what you have accumulated and can deploy A capital inventory consists of listing what capitals of each type you have and whether/ how you would deploy them for impact. To bring these possibilities to life, it is useful to understand the qualities of capitals. Earlier sections outlined the types of capital as: ⁕ Economic (money and assets) ⁕ Social (relationships - quality and quantity) ⁕ Cultural (know-how from professional or personal experience), and ⁕ Symbolic (reputation as an individual or member of a group).

YOUR CAPITALS

Other important questions to consider when creating your inventory of capitals and how deployable they are:

Where does capital “end up” when spent? Sometimes capital returns to the original owner (e.g., your economic ROI), whereas other types and situations return to both the owner and other parties15 (e.g., your and others' social capital increases when you introduce people to one another). 37

Can it change hands? Some capital can be given to others (e.g. donating money) while others can be used without giving it away16 (e.g., using cultural capital to mentor someone).

Can it be changed into other types of capital? Some types of capital, like money or other physical objects, are easier to convert17 (e.g., paying for a Master’s degree converts economic capital into cultural capital), while cultural capital, for example, is less easily or directly converted18.

Creating your capital inventory

S TE P 2

Determine what to use for impact Using information from the prior section, you can imagine creating a long list of capitals you have at your disposal. However, there are many capitals you may not want to allocate for impact. For example, many wealth holders may not want to use their symbolic capital, associating their names publicly with a cause. Similarly, the capitals you have and want to utilize may vary by cause or your theory of change, if you have one. All capital types require time to deploy. In the framework, your capital inventory and your impact focus are presented concurrently because they are deeply interrelated. The impact focus you choose will determine who you are engaging with and the complementary capitals these individuals and others contribute to shared impact objectives.

Update your inventory regularly The inventory you create today reflects the current moment in time. Some of your capitals may endure over time (e.g. knowledge acquired from an MBA), but many are not static. Your inventory will change over time as: ⁕ Some capitals grow

(e.g., your reputation as an impact investor) ⁕ Others diminish (e.g., an allocation of philanthropic dollars) ⁕ New capitals are acquired

All of this means that it is essential to update your inventory periodically. 39

Defining your impact focus With an initial capital inventory in mind, consider your impact focus. Impact focus refers to the process by which you choose the areas your multicapital strategies will serve. You will undoubtedly notice, as you consider your areas of interest, that more capitals occur to you, or that certain capitals from your initial inventory will not be useful in specific areas. The capital inventory, impact focus and systems awareness processes should be both iterative and interrelated.

S TE P 1

Consider capital inventory and impact focus overlap We advocate for conducting a capital inventory prior to narrowing your impact focus, because it often helps people to see their resources in a new light, without the narrowing effect of past and current projects. However, for people deeply engaged in or committed to a particular area, it may be appropriate to dig into particulars of their impact focus prior to inventorying their capital. Regardless of the order, conducting an inventory and selecting an impact focus are essential ingredients for an informed capital deployment strategy.

Developing your systems awareness The capital inventory and impact focus sections center the capital holder identifying capitals, individual passions and interests and how you may combine these to positively contribute. The systems awareness phase brings these elements into alignment with the world where deployment will happen. Together, these three elements inform the deployment strategy. See the Investor's Guide to Systemic Investing for more on systems awareness: cspglobal.org/research/publications/ investors-guide-systemic-investing S TE P 1

Conduct an evidence review Once you have narrowed your impact focus, determine the best way to contribute. This requires evidence regarding the system you plan to invest in, so that you can optimize your contribution relative to initiatives and expertise already at work. As you conduct your evidence review, consider: Scientific evidence These sources may range from academic literature reviews to journalism, impact reports, and systems maps. You will need different types of evidence depending on the contribution you want to make. As you conduct your review, be sure to consider evidence regarding relevant factors such as urgency or scale of the intervention. Communities of practice Experts working in communities of practice and other proximate leaders20 have unique and valuable lived experience that can inform how you shape your impact focus. 42
