05 Map the Impact

of Your Assets

To begin a transition to impact, families can start by understanding the social and environmental impact—both positive and negative—of their current assets. This involves examining multiple layers of asset ownership, from the legal structures that hold their wealth to the specific activities of each company they are invested in. For families with operating businesses, it also means assessing the impact of their core operations and business practices.

Embed purpose into structure

Learning through feedback

Creating a structure that embeds purpose and intent ensures that a family’s values and long-term vision are consistently reflected in how decisions are made and resources are deployed.

Getting feedback from partners and investees can enable a family to deepen their understanding of their own impact as an investor and partner, and build stronger relationships. For example, Happiness Capital engages the external firm IPSOS to survey their portfolio companies on their experiences working with them, highlighting where they are performing well as a funder and where they can strengthen their support.

For example, Ishk Tolaram Foundation is designated as a beneficiary of the Tolaram Family Trust, solidifying its founder’s commitment to giving and impact. Another example is Chavalit Frederick Tsao, Chairman of TPC (Tsao Pao Chee), who fully vested his business interest from a privately owned company into a trust in 2015, culminating from “a long process of engagement, healing, and shifting consciousness in showing that we are committed to impact.”

Weave Impact into Due Diligence

To incorporate impact into investment decisions, investors add a layer of analysis of the social and environmental value a company can create, and social and environmental risks inherent to the company’s products, services, and operations. Families often rely on external advisors or service providers to assess both potential value creation and risks. Families may also include an assessment of experiential return and risk to their due diligence, assessing the value they may derive from the learning experience and the potential reputational risk of a given investment.

Additional Resources

Assess “Theory of Change” Determining why and how an enterprise or a fund is expected to bring about desired changes (what is commonly referred to as a theory of change) can be a useful step in a family’s due diligence process. “We look at what needs to go in and work in order for that theory of change to materialize. We ask quite in-depth questions to assess the mechanics of operationalizing their impact model,” said Divya Patel, Chief Executive Officer of Ishk Tolaram Foundation.

Collaborate on due diligence Families can take a collaborative approach to due diligence by engaging relevant parties—whether co-investors, subject matter experts, or even the portfolio companies themselves. Jian Li Yew, Chief Executive Officer of Citrine Capital, exemplifies this through a practice of open due diligence with potential portfolio companies: “We share a substantial portion of our draft investment memo directly with the company. This gives them the opportunity to correct inaccuracies, add additional context, and respond to any concerns we’ve raised. They often value the depth and rigour of our analysis. For example, our competitive landscape review often revealed players they hadn’t previously identified, and our profiling of key team members has surfaced discrepancies they were not aware of. Together, we refine the memo to ensure it is accurate and built on mutual understanding—before finalising it for internal review.”

Reference existing frameworks A family can use existing frameworks as a way to broadly categorize and assess high-level intentions and potential impact of an investment opportunity. These can then be connected to more granular impact and data categories, which help a family to measure and manage its impact.

07 Build and Manage

a Portfolio

Building an impact portfolio involves sourcing opportunities, making informed investment decisions, structuring deals, and offering ongoing support. Building a strong impact portfolio becomes more manageable when families collaborate with a trusted network of like-minded partners.

Seek values-aligned investees In the same vein to building a values-aligned team, some families also examine an investee’s philosophy and decision-making behaviour. For example, Bryan Goh, Chief Executive Officer of Tsao Family Office, explained that they “often engage in open-ended discussions where there are no clear answers within the team and with external managers. The goal is to see whether they’ve grappled with these complex questions themselves—not necessarily to get a definitive answer, but to understand the depth of their thinking.”

Leverage business expertise

“

Families with established operating businesses often possess deep industry knowledge and networks. By focusing on sectors closely related to their core enterprise, they can deploy capital more confidently and effectively.

Our investment thesis has evolved. We began by mastering the building blocks of the industrial world— building materials—which gave us an understanding of its real-world complexities. Adopting sustainability as a core lens for investment has fundamentally shaped our strategy. It has taught us to apply our deep operational expertise not just to what is profitable today, but to what is essential and enduring for tomorrow.

Our focus is on two interconnected fronts. The first is investing in the critical technologies and infrastructure for industrial decarbonization and the energy transition. The second is deploying capital into the scalable software and technology platforms that will act as the great accelerator. In an age where the digital divide is set to widen, we believe technology is the key to ensuring our foundational industries are not just participants, but leaders

in this new era. It’s about democratizing impact and efficiency. We’ve moved beyond optimizing a single enterprise to catalyzing an entire ecosystem, building the technological and sustainable foundations for the future.” Kelvin Fu Managing Partner Gunung Capital

Measure and Manage Impact To evaluate progress and success, families clarify how they measure and assess impact alongside financial performance. A variety of impact measurement and management frameworks exist, designed to help companies understand the consequences of their products and operations, and to help investors understand the outcomes created by the deployment of their capital.

Leverage established impact frameworks Families can build their own customized impact management tool by referencing existing databases of impact metrics, such as the Impact Management Project, IRIS Catalogue of Metrics, or the SDG Impact Standards. These resources provide a foundation for families to maintain consistency and comparability while tailoring the tool to their specific goals—without having to start from scratch.

Use external verification External verification and reporting tools can help families assess and benchmark impact and ESG practices across their investments. For example, the Tsao Family Office uses BlueMark, as both investor and client of Bluemark, uses its new Fund ID tool to benchmark funds during due diligence and in post-investment reporting, gaining comparable and objective data.

Join an impact measurement program Cohort-based impact measurement programs—such as those run by Impact Frontiers that RS Group participated in—can help investors strengthen their impact management practices by working alongside peers. These programs support participants in building or refining their frameworks, processes, and systems to fully integrate impact considerations into investment decision-making, manager engagement, and monitoring process.

“

We’ve conducted extensive research into existing frameworks and metrics—some were useful, others less so. Drawing from the most relevant and developing our own where needed, we curated an impact framework based on our five impact pillars of health and wellbeing. Each pillar includes three key metrics, giving us a total of 15. Any healthcare companies we assess, whether public or private, typically align with at least three to five of these. This framework forms the foundation of our impact evaluation approach.”

09 Engage Financial

Institutions

Many families rely on external institutional wealth managers or asset management firms to implement their impact strategies. By actively engaging these partners, they boost the chances of meeting their goals and can help raise industry standards for impact investing.

Actively engage fund managers Active engagement and building trusted relationships with managers allow families to build deeper alignment throughout the investment process. Some families use regular constructive dialogue, while others conduct more formal annual reviews.

Seed new impact products Some families actively engage with managers to seed new impact-aligned products. They help shape fund strategy and impact goals from the outset, while leveraging the scale and infrastructure of established managers to bring impact into mainstream investing. For example, the Tsao Family Office co-developed funds—like Invesco’s ESG loan fund, embedding impact processes and enabling offerings that would not otherwise exist. They also have been an early investor in impactful products such as Wellington’s Global Impact Bond Fund, thereby helping to create a critical mass of capital to enable the product to garner further investment from other investors.

Support the Impact Ecosystem

Like any other growing field, the impact investing market requires more than capital allocation—it requires an ecosystem. This ecosystem can be supported by families through funding, expertise, and networks. Ultimately, this work increases the likelihood that a family can make increasingly higher quality impact investments in the future. We saw that the eight families supported the development of new frameworks and other ecosystem building efforts. Here are some examples. Happiness Capital developed and shared the Happiness Return Framework with other investors to be adapted to other impact goals. To further thought leadership and build an ecosystem around wellbeing, sustainability, and family business legacy, Chavalit Frederick Tsao launched several organizations under TPC (Tsao Pao Chee), including OCTAVE Living, OCTAVE Capital (formerly known as Heritas Capital), and the three affiliated non-profit entities for TPC: OCTAVE Institute, Restore Nature Foundation and NO.17 Foundation. TPC also organizes Impact Week in Singapore, a catalytic festival where business, philanthropy, capital, and community come together to reimagine the systems that serve life. To further support small family businesses and enterprises (SMEs), TPC has also set up the Association for Well-being Economy HK Chapter to provide impact programmes to these SMEs such that they can do well and do good. Citrine Capital contributed to the formation and ongoing work of the Malaysia Impact Alliance (MYImpact), the Malaysian National Partner of Global Steering Group for Impact Investing (GSG Impact). Collaborating closely with partners across diverse sectors and industries, Citrine Capital co-created MYImpact’s mission: to catalyze the Malaysia’s impact economy by driving insightful awareness and practical action for system change. PT Gunung Raja Paksi Tbk is advancing steel innovation and broader efforts to pursue lower-carbon emissions in the steel industry through active engagement of external stakeholders and participating in key dialogues and initiatives such as the World Steel Association, World Economic Forum, South East Asia Iron and Steel Institute, Indonesia’s Green Label Product Certification, and Indonesia’s National Dialogue on Accelerating Green Economy Transformation. RS Group supports the development of systemic investing frameworks such as those by Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth (CSP). Hanson Gong also supports the development of systemic investing pioneers such as those by Transformation Capital (TransCap), TWIST (Together We Invest for Systems Change) as well as research through MIT and Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth (CSP). Families also seed and support networks. For example, Chavalit Frederick Tsao seeded the Asian Chapter of the Family Business Network and is currently the Chairman of Family Business Network Impact Committee/Council of Wisdom, encouraging family businesses to put impact in the center of all their business strategies, as well as joining the Global Impact Investing Network (GIIN) Investors’ Council.

About this guide

A goals-based approach to investing and philanthropy is built on the recognition that capital is a means, not an end. In traditional investing, this challenges the assumption that maximizing wealth is the ultimate objective. Instead, it recognizes that capital is merely an instrument; the true goal is the intrinsic value—such as financial security or a life of well-being—that this capital can help achieve. This distinction is increasingly central well beyond private wealth, including in institutional investing and public policy. It is an equally crucial distinction for impact investing and philanthropy. Without clear goals, investors risk merely funding activities rather than real progress. By bringing the rigorous focus of a goals-based approach to their impact allocations, investors can move from simply “doing good” to generating specific, meaningful improvements in the world. This guide makes the case that before diving into detailed strategies, structures, or investments, it is crucial to clarify what you are trying to accomplish. While this may seem obvious, our experience working with hundreds of investors shows that unclear or conflicting goals often lead to disappointing results and wasted time. Drawing on insights from academic research and the real-world experiences of investors and their families, this guide outlines the work necessary to move beyond inherited assumptions and focus on what actually matters to you. Clarifying your goals sets the stage for deploying your resources to more effectively achieve all your goals—whether financial, personal, or about generating a positive impact on the world.

PARTNERS

CENTER FOR SUSTAINABLE FINANCE AND PRIVATE WEALTH (CSP)

Spun out of Harvard University in 2017, CSP is a vibrant network of wealth holders, researchers, educators, and entrepreneurs committed to making private wealth a force for good. Our research and training empower private investors, philanthropists, inheritors, and their advisors to achieve greater and more systemic environmental and social impact using all their forms of capital. We operate globally with teams based in the U.S., Switzerland, and Singapore. We work closely with the MIT Sloan School of Management Sustainability Initiative and the Stanford Center on Philanthropy and Civil Society.

Investor’s Guide to Goals-based Investing and Philanthropy

Foreword

Dr. Falko Paetzold Founder, CSP; Managing Director, CCSP-HSG Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth & HSG

This guide emerged from a simple observation: many investors struggle to make progress on their social and environmental impact goals (or their financial goals) simply because they haven’t clearly defined them.

Dr. Vera Michalchik Senior Research Scholar and Director Stanford PACS

Dr. Jason Jay Senior Lecturer and Director MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative

Mike McCreless Founder and Executive Director Impact Frontiers

Dr. Jonathan Harris Senior Fellow Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth & HSG

While many investors and philanthropists are driven to make a difference, we have observed that they often feel overwhelmed and unsure where to start. What they need isn’t another set of rigid prescriptions. This guide is built on a simple premise: investors need to give themselves permission to clarify their goals. Doing so is valuable whether you are just starting out or feeling stuck in a strategic rut. Indeed, if your current strategy feels stale or reactive, revisiting your goals can quickly unlock new energy. The insights shared here don’t tell you what goals to pursue or how much to prioritize each one. While your specific priorities may be unique, the fundamental challenges of balancing multiple objectives and making coherent decisions in a complex, dynamic world are universal. We offer practical steps you can apply again and again to sharpen your thinking throughout your journey, helping you to better shape your investment and philanthropic strategies.

Traditional approaches often begin by narrowing interests to a few “focus areas.” Yet investors inherently juggle multiple financial and impact goals. When these are forced together, depth is often lost. For example, an investor might attempt to satisfy a deep desire for impact with a generic ESG screen. To avoid this, we advocate for focused structures—dedicated allocations of resources—that enable you to pursue multiple goals in a coherent manner. This guide focuses on essential groundwork: clarifying your various goals, understanding how different opportunities serve those goals, and organizing your resources to best reach them while managing the inevitable complexities. All investors approach these steps with different values and perspectives; however, working through them allows you to move beyond inherited assumptions and deploy your capital more purposefully. The world needs diverse approaches to solving its problems. The most exciting possibility isn’t that we all adopt the same approach to impact, but that we each find our most effective way to contribute. We hope this guide helps you navigate that path with confidence.

Identify your goals

Plan your approach

Start with foundational work. Every investor has a multitude of goals, constraints, and opportunities (Insight 1). It is important to clarify your goals to bring structure to this complexity: understand that each goal acts as a unique lens through which you evaluate opportunities (Insight 2). A deeper understanding of your own goals also enables you to better grasp other stakeholders’ perspectives and coordinate with others to achieve win-win results.

The clarity that comes from identifying your goals helps you ensure coherence in your decision-making, so you don’t leave value on the table (Insight 3). You can support this coherence by creating focused structures: dedicated allocations of capital and resources toward specific priorities (Insight 4). Ultimately, a coherent approach gives you the best possible chance of achieving your goals.

Implement your plan

Learn and evolve

This guide serves as a reminder of the importance of clear goals for implementation, but it is not about the dynamic work of implementation itself. There is a wide range of excellent materials on implementation, and some of these are highlighted throughout the guide.

With a clear and coherent foundation in place, your focus can shift to improvement and growth. This deep, ongoing learning is what ultimately unlocks advanced strategies (Insight 5), allowing you to create a deeper impact while ensuring your goals evolve as you engage with the world (Insight 6).

Paolo’s coherence checks Julie’s “buckets”enable ensure every investment her to pursue different earns its place goals effectively

Max Zeller studied mechanical engineering and felt a general pull toward clean tech, but he soon realized that a vague interest wasn’t enough to drive real change. He narrowed his focus relentlessly until he landed on a single, specific thesis: carbon removal. This clarity allowed him to bypass generalist distractions and build a specialized venture firm, Carbon Removal Partners.

Paolo Fresia applies a rigorous “opportunity cost” logic to his wealth to ensure his investing and philanthropy are coherent. For example, if an investment offers higher risk or lower returns, he asks: “Is the impact I’m ‘buying’ with that actually worth more than the climate mitigation I could buy with a simple grant?”

“I

t felt so logical to me that this is the direction we need to go. Focusing deep on one topic gives you the credibility to actually get things done.”

Max’s journey illustrates that focusing on a specific goal doesn’t limit your impact; it deepens your expertise, making you a magnet for the specific opportunities that matter most. 10

“I

try to compare the impact of my investments directly against the impact of the best charities. If the investment can’t beat the charity on impact efficiency, I don’t make excuses for it.”

Paolo’s approach creates a competition for capital across his total portfolio, ensuring every tool makes a net positive contribution to his goals.

Julie Engelhorn manages a diverse set of goals by maintaining distinct, focused structures for each, including one for catalytic investing, one for systemic investing, an allocation to highleverage philanthropy, and a personal bucket for her family and regenerative farming projects.

“I

realized I didn’t need one strategy to rule them all. I needed different vehicles for different kinds of impact, and the freedom to manage them differently.”

The Finks’ shift to food waste addressed a neglected crisis

Hanson Gong began his journey inspired simply by Tikkun Olam (the concept of repairing the world), but as he engaged deeper, he realized that funding one company at a time often failed to address root causes. He realized lasting impact would require shifting the system itself. This goal led him to systemic investing.

Betsy and Jesse Fink were early pioneers in climate change investing through MissionPoint Capital Partners, but as capital flooded into renewable energy, they realized their contribution was shrinking. Around the same time, Betsy’s experience with farming led them to food waste, a then-neglected driver of emissions that was receiving little attention. They co-founded ReFED to build the field from scratch.

“T

o repair the world, you have to understand how it is broken. Systemic investing allows us to target the root causes rather than just treating the symptoms.”

Hanson’s evolution highlights that advanced strategies are not just intellectual exercises; they are the necessary tools for investors whose goals have moved beyond symptoms to roots.

e need to go where the capital isn’t. Food waste was where climate change was 15 years before, a massive opportunity that everyone was overlooking.”

INSIGHT

Clear goals are foundational

1 NTIFY IDE

As Paul Brest and Hal Harvey argue in their book Money Well Spent, a smart strategy built on clear goals is central to generating significant positive impact.1 This isn’t just motivational fluff; it’s backed by decades of research showing that specific, challenging goals significantly boost performance compared to vague intentions like “doing your best.” 2 This guide takes its title from “goalsbased investing.” 3 This means managing wealth not simply to maximize returns (e.g., a certain amount in your account), but to achieve real-world outcomes that contribute to an investor’s well-being (e.g., a certain lifestyle, after accounting for inflation). For example, Nobel laureate Robert Merton at MIT has made this point for retirement planning, and Stanford’s John Cochrane makes a similar point for long-horizon investors by focusing on what a portfolio can actually pay for over time. The idea of a goals-based approach also applies to more philanthropic pursuits. It comes down to one question: “What are the ultimate outcomes I am trying to achieve with my capital?”

The power of specific goals Here, we use “goals” as an umbrella term for everything from high-level missions to precise, tactical targets. At any level, a goal is only useful if it is specific enough to guide your choices when trade-offs arise. Sport is the clearest example: structured goal setting improves performance.4 Clarity helps under pressure For investors, the challenge isn’t just the multitude of potential goals to choose from; it’s also the constant barrage of external pressures. Advisors may push for a simplistic focus on a single metric, while peers advocate for their own favored causes. Both can feel incomplete because they fail to account for an investor’s core identity, moral commitments, and relationships.5 In the face of these pressures, clear goals make it easier to evaluate advice and peer input.

Insight 1

Illustrated story: Alice Figure 2 provides a framework to help clarify and understand any goal. While it draws inspiration from frameworks like Impact Frontiers’ five dimensions of impact, originally developed by the Impact Management Project (IMP), it is uniquely focused on goals.

Effective investors set instrumental goals: smaller, manageable targets that serve as stepping stones toward a larger objective. Yet, these instrumental goals are not ends in themselves, and this distinction is important to keep in mind.

To illustrate, imagine Alice, an investor who has just inherited a significant fortune. Table 1 on the next page shows three of her core goals mapped to the dimensions. Three of these dimensions deserve special attention. The WHY dimension clarifies a goal’s purpose: is it an end in itself (intrinsic) or a means to a larger end (instrumental)? While your intrinsic goals may be ambitious and long-term, success often requires breaking them down.

The RISK dimension captures the level of certainty required: is the goal essential (must be achieved) or aspirational (ambitious, but failure can be tolerated)? Finally, the HOW MUCH dimension defines the nature of the goal. Is it satisficing (aiming for “enough”) or maximizing (aiming for the best possible)? Ultimately, treat your goals as hypotheses along these dimensions— provisional yet action-guiding views on what is valuable to you. They should evolve as you learn and grow.

Insight 1

Clarifying your essential financial goals: how much is enough? For many investors, the default financial goal is simply “more.” This vague aim, often reinforced by advisors, can create issues both personally and systemically. On a personal level, it can create persistent anxiety about never having enough. At a systemic level, a relentless focus on accumulation creates its own set of complex challenges. The Enough Project, founded by Brent Kessel and Robert Boogaard, offers a powerful alternative by asking a different question: “How much is enough?” Their process encourages a thoughtful exploration of wealth, impact, and wellbeing, centered on three core elements:

Having enough

Doing enough

Being enough

This involves a structured process of working out how much you actually need for your desired lifestyle and loved ones. By replacing the drive for endless accumulation with a concrete number, you can gain financial clarity and a genuine sense of security.

Once you define “enough,” you can unlock your “surplus.” This allows resources that aren’t required for that goal to be deployed in line with the world’s needs, enabling a meaningful contribution to tackling pressing problems.

Wisdom traditions teach us that relying on external validation can create a cycle of endless wanting.6 By refusing to define yourself by what you have or what you do, you can better focus on balancing your own needs with serving the world. As illustrated in the story of “Alice” in Insight 4, this structured exploration is not about limiting ambition. Defining “enough” creates clarity and psychological freedom, empowering you to pursue more ambitious impact goals with conviction.

Insight 1

The power of moral ambition

What is an “impact goal”?

Research shows that setting specific, challenging goals drives superior performance. This insight becomes particularly relevant when considering the scale of ambition in the world of impact.

This guide’s framework can help you with any type of goal, but it’s particularly useful for investors looking to create positive change. So, what defines an “impact goal”?

Historian Rutger Bregman champions the idea of “moral ambition.” He contrasts the common drive for personal success or wealth with an ambition that seeks to apply skills and resources to tackling the world’s biggest problems. It’s about treating “doing good” with the same intensity and strategic rigor as personal achievement. This concept ties directly into the distinction between essential and aspirational goals. While you might set clear and challenging essential goals for your financial security, the idea of moral ambition encourages you to set equally robust aspirational goals for your impact. It pushes you to think bigger about your potential contributions.

For our purposes, an impact goal is simply any goal focused primarily on “others”—such as a community, society, or the planet. It can be an intrinsic goal (where the outcome for others is the end in itself) or an instrumental goal that supports such intrinsic aims. This distinguishes impact goals from values-alignment goals, which often overlap but not always. Investors who prioritize impact goals tend to focus on several key principles: Contribution: When the goal is to benefit others, the key question becomes: “Did my actions create a real positive change that wouldn’t have happened otherwise?” The attribution for that change becomes secondary to whether the change actually occurred.

Systems Awareness: Helping others solve problems often requires understanding the complex system in which they exist, including potential unintended consequences. This reduces the risk of unintended harm and helps identify the highest-leverage ways to help. Stakeholder Perspective: Finally, a focus on outcomes for others requires you to understand what those “others” actually value. This means engaging with stakeholders to grasp their values and appetite for risk, ensuring your strategy aligns with their needs rather than just your assumptions. As noted earlier, specific goals drive superior performance. However, applying this logic to impact is inherently challenging. Unlike a race time or a bank balance, impact is multi-dimensional and often difficult to assess. Managing impact well demands a high level of selfawareness and a willingness to iterate. See Insight 6 for a discussion of how goals evolve.

INSIGHT

Even tiny differences in goals can be big in practice

2 NTIFY IDE

Each of your goals acts like a unique lens, shaping how you perceive and evaluate opportunities. The same investment can look attractive through one lens and irrelevant through another. This matters because your impact often scales with the size of your coalition. You cannot coordinate effectively with others until you are clear about what you aim to achieve. Even a slight shift in a goal’s definition can lead to completely different opportunities becoming the priority. For example, a goal to “help kids now” might lead one to fund malaria bed nets, a proven, high-certainty solution. A goal to “help future kids,” however, might lead to funding higher-risk medical research and development (R&D). To an outsider, both goals are “helping kids.”

But the difference in the “WHEN” dimension creates two vastly different portfolios, networks, and sets of required expertise. Even when people share a goal, they can disagree sharply about the means, for example, private action versus policy change. This is the root of why wellintentioned people—family members, board members, and advisors—so often disagree. Much of what we call strategy is the subjective act of choosing which lens to apply. As Figure 3 illustrates, filtering the same opportunities through different goal lenses can produce very different assessments of what is “best.”

Insight 2

Illustrated story: Alice’s cousin, Bob

Diversity in perspectives doesn’t have to be a problem; it can be a source of strength. As the old parable reminds us, when several blind men try to describe an elephant, each has a valid but incomplete perspective. Complex social and environmental problems are the same; they are too vast to be understood through a single lens. The world needs diverse perspectives to solve its problems. The challenge, then, is not to force everyone to see the world the same way. It’s about recognizing our own lenses and learning to engage constructively with those who view the world differently. Consider Alice and her cousin, Bob.7 Despite sharing a goal to improve global health through their family foundation, they often find themselves in conflict, unable to approve any significant grants, and straining their personal relationship. 22

Navigating Gridlock When a group of people with different lenses tries to make a decision, the result is often “gridlock”—either persistent conflict or avoidance of the topic. In their book Breaking Through Gridlock, Jason Jay and Gabriel Grant argue that the way forward isn’t to quarrel over the “facts” of an investment, but to engage in structured conversations about the underlying lenses. Conversations get stuck when we become attached to being “right” and see others as “resistant.” The key is to notice this attachment and separate disagreements about goals from disagreements about methods. Ground yourself in what you truly want (both progress on your goal and a healthy relationship), and then shift to a space of curiosity and inquiry.

From there, ask questions to understand what the other person values, what their goals are, and why those goals matter to them. This shared understanding creates a foundation for a creative search for “win-win” options—new investment ideas that can achieve both sets of objectives, rather than assuming a simple trade-off. Move from asking “What are my goals and values?” to asking “What goals do I share with a coalition strong enough to achieve them together?”

Insight 2

Illustrated story: Alice’s cousin, Bob

Diversity in perspectives doesn’t have to be a problem; it can be a source of strength. As the old parable reminds us, when several blind men try to describe an elephant, each has a valid but incomplete perspective. INSIGHT

Without coherence, you leave value on the table

3 PLAN

Choosing which goals to prioritize is a personal, often moral, decision. However, once you select your goals, you can assess your actions against a clear standard: coherence. While no one can dictate your values, anyone can assess if your decisions align with them. What “coherence” means Even if you’re uncertain about your values, or how to act on them, you can control whether your decisions fit together and reflect the same values. You can debate goals on moral grounds, but coherence is about whether your actions match the goals you claim to have. If your choices are a muddled reflection of your priorities, they won’t effectively represent what you care about. In that case, you risk leaving value on the table according to your own criteria. Many investors and philanthropists are less coherent than they think, often for understandable reasons: committees, legacy commitments, and the complexity

of impact. Another common reason is discomfort with explicitly managing trade-offs—stating priorities, saying no, and ranking opportunities. The cost is hidden but real: less progress toward your goals. That’s why having clear goals (Insight 1) is essential; vague inputs make coherence challenging. For example, consider an investor who practices disciplined philanthropy. If they accept lower financial returns in their impact investing portfolio for ambiguous impact claims—claims that wouldn’t pass their grant committee—they risk being incoherent. By accepting a financial loss for inadequate impact, they effectively make a grant that doesn’t align with their standards—money that could have been used better elsewhere.

Coherence vs incoherence

PRIORITY 1 PRIORITY 2

COHERENCE

INCOHERENCE

Coherent competition for capital

Trade-offs: A universal challenge

Once you have clear goals, the most effective investors and philanthropists seek to maintain what we call a “coherent competition for capital.” 8 This concept has two key parts. First, competition means every opportunity must continuously prove its worth against all other options.

Trade-offs are often uncomfortable, which is why many investors keep their goals vague or treat each investment as a stand-alone decision. But ignoring trade-offs doesn’t make them vanish; it only leads to poor management.

Second, coherence means applying the same values and rules consistently across all opportunities in that competition. It’s this blend—a comprehensive competition and consistent criteria—that creates an effective process.

Even an investor who believes they only fund “win-win” opportunities cannot escape this reality. Given two excellent investments, they still have to choose which one is the best use of capital. Furthermore, even for a foundation devoted to a single impact goal, there is a fundamental trade-off to manage: creating impact now (i.e., through grants) versus generating financial returns to support greater impact in the future.

Insight 3

Participants at the ‘‘Impact Investing for the Next Generation’’ training in Boston, MA.

Making trade-offs explicit in practice Julie Sunderland, then founding director of program-related investments (PRI) at the Gates Foundation, described in the Stanford Social Innovation Review how her team managed this impact-financial trade-off in practice.9 When considering an investment in a high-impact, highrisk venture, they essentially asked: “Is the impact we expect this investment to generate worth the expected financial cost, compared to what an alternative grant could achieve?” The investment team defined the “risk share”—the expected cost of an investment compared to more commercial alternatives. Then, the grantmaking team assessed whether this expected cost was a wise use of the foundation’s capital. If so, they funded the risk share from their budget. This wasn’t just an accounting trick; it was a way to make investment decisions that consistently reflected their grantmaking strategy. Impact valuation The “risk share” approach relates to a growing strategic tool: impact valuation. This is the practice of making the importance of an investment’s impacts clear by expressing them in a common metric. This helps manage trade-offs and guide decision-making. 29

In this example, an investment being worth its “risk share” implies that its impact is at least as important as the outcomes the foundation could generate with an alternative grant. Impact valuation is a core component of the broader practice of impact-financial integration, which aims to manage impact and financial performance together in a single, coherent way. Visual coherence: Alice’s process Figure 5 (following page) shows how Alice approaches her Pandemic Preparedness strategy. She starts with a set of opportunities and assigns financial and impact scores to each one. The figure then presents the potential selections Alice could make based on different trade-offs between the financial and impact scores. As the figure shows, the most effective portfolios lie on the “impact frontier,” meaning they offer the best possible impact given a target financial score.10 These frontier portfolios are built from a coherent selection of opportunities— their choices can be explained by a single, consistent rule. Incoherent portfolios fall below this frontier, and their messy mix of decisions leaves value on the table.

Putting coherence into practice Coherent valuation emphasizes the importance of directing your time and energy toward the highest-stakes decisions. It’s more effective to focus on significant trade-offs than to get bogged down in minor choices, like picking between similar ESG ETFs. While a detailed quantitative process can feel overwhelming, the main principle boils down to two straightforward questions: ⁕ If this investment has “below market”

returns, does its combination of impact and financial return make it a better choice than an alternative investment or grant? ⁕ If this investment offers competitive returns and generates a significant impact, can I increase my allocation to it? As the examples of Alice and others in the subsequent “Different Paths to Coherence” section reveal, creating a method to answer these questions provides strategic clarity and inspiration for many investors. Different paths to coherence Coherent management is not one-size-fits-all; it depends on context, shaped by an investor’s expertise and available opportunities. Here are three distinct but coherent paths for investors dedicated to generating positive impact.

PATH 1

PATH 2

PATH 3

Allow yourself to stop

Build an edge

Build a disciplined process

One CSP alum’s journey led them to become a leader in grantmaking focused on extreme poverty. To complement this work, they ventured into impact investing. However, they found the available advisors did not offer investment opportunities that matched the high quality of the grant proposals they reviewed daily. Moreover, these options came with high administrative costs, which made them inconsistent with their main impact goals. They chose to pause their exploration of impact investing—a pragmatic decision to focus their resources where they could generate the greatest impact.

In contrast, Jochem Wieringa, with a background in venture capital, took an investment-oriented approach to create his own unique edge. He invested years in developing deep investment contacts across Africa, allowing him to avoid reliance on intermediaries and tap into a wealth of neglected opportunities. These investments benefit stakeholders similar to those in the CSP alum’s work, yet provide a compelling mix of impact and high returns. He keeps his focus on leveraging his specialized access, using an impact valuation approach to ensure a clear competition for capital across all opportunities, including the best grants.

Another CSP alum, Paolo Fresia, employs his own impact valuation method to maintain clear competition for capital, even without a specialized edge. He uses both quantitative and qualitative criteria to assess his options, enabling him to make coherent trade-offs. For instance, he can directly compare a grant to a climate charity with a loan to a regenerative agriculture project and an equity investment in a green-tech company. This structured approach ensures every dollar is allocated in a way that best serves his impact goals.

Moreover, these options came with high administrative costs, which made them inconsistent with their main impact goals. They chose to pause their exploration of impact investing—a pragmatic decision to focus their resources where they could generate the greatest impact.

In contrast, Jochem Wieringa, with a background in venture capital, took an investment-oriented approach to create his own unique edge. He invested years in developing deep investment contacts across Africa, allowing him to avoid reliance on intermediaries and tap into a wealth of neglected opportunities. These investments benefit stakeholders similar to those in the CSP alum’s work, yet provide a compelling mix of impact and high returns. He keeps his focus on leveraging his specialized access, using an impact valuation approach to ensure a clear competition for capital across all opportunities, including the best grants.

Another CSP alum, Paolo Fresia, employs his own impact valuation method to maintain clear competition for capital, even without a specialized edge. He uses both quantitative and qualitative criteria to assess his options, enabling him to make coherent trade-offs. For instance, he can directly compare a grant to a climate charity with a loan to a regenerative agriculture project and an equity investment in a green-tech company. This structured approach ensures every dollar is allocated in a way that best serves his impact goals.

Where coherence breaks

Ultimately, it comes down to clarity on your goals and how you prioritize them. INSIGHT

Pursue goals separately to enable coherence

PLAN

Balancing multiple goals at once can be challenging and often unproductive. We all have limited attention and decision-making capacity (“bounded rationality”). A general solution is to create focused structures. The benefits of focus

DEFINING FOCUSED STRUCTURES

The purpose of focused structures is twofold: to manage conflicts and harness synergies. By separating unrelated goals (like financial security and global health), you can turn what often feels like a constant juggling act into occasional, high-level decisions.

A focused structure is an active, dedicated allocation of capital, resources, and activities toward a specific set of goals. Effective structures share several key features:

Grouping related goals creates a dedicated space to cultivate potential synergies. The resulting sense of harmony, where conflicts between goals are managed and outweighed by strong synergies, has been shown to be a strong predictor of a goalsetter’s persistence, performance, and well-being.11

⁕ They serve related goals. Goals whose activities interact— whether through conflict or synergy— are best managed together.

⁕ They have defined priorities. Each structure has clear priorities that allow for a coherent competition for capital within it.

⁕ They separate unrelated goals. Goals that are unrelated are best separated to allow for focused execution in parallel. ⁕ They can be formal or informal. A structure can be a distinct legal entity, like a trust or foundation, or simply a “mental account.”

Insight 4

Wisdom from daily life

Constraints and opportunities

Think of it like organizing your time. Dedicating blocks for work, family, and health allows you to be fully present and effective in each area. This strategy is far superior to attempting to multitask everything at once. This separation lets you apply a focused approach within each block, enhancing decision-making and reducing paralysis.

In practice, these structures also need to account for real-world constraints and opportunities. A legal trust with strict limitations is a constraint that naturally imposes a structure. Your unique expertise in a specific industry is an opportunity that might define another structure. Beyond asset classes

Or consider how we separate retirement savings from daily cash. We create distinct structures (like pension funds) to protect a specific long-term goal from short-term competing pressures. Applying this same logic to your impact goals—separating your “safety” bucket from your “moonshot” bucket—is the most reliable way to ensure you don’t accidentally sacrifice one for the other. 37

Traditional advisors organize around asset classes (e.g., stocks, bonds, real estate). The shift to goals-based investing is simple but profound: instead of organizing around these asset classes, you organize around what actually matters to you (e.g., security, impact, legacy).

Structuring for essentials

These examples highlight the essence of goals-based investing. Building on the work of Nobel laureates like Richard Thaler (on “mental accounting”) and Herbert Simon (on “bounded rationality”), practitioners like Ashvin Chhabra have shown that investors can achieve better outcomes by aligning distinct pools of capital with clear, distinct goals.3 By creating a focused structure for her essential goals, Alice had unlocked the freedom to be more ambitious with her surplus.

Alice began by identifying her essential goals as in Insight 1: “Financial Security” and “Creative Expression.” To create focused structures and strategies, she needed to drill down further. Using the “enough” process, she established specific targets for her Financial Security. For Creative Expression, she decided to focus on her passion for music. This led to two distinct structures: a conservative portfolio for her financial security and a dedicated studio and budget for her music. Because of her wealth, neither structure demanded an excessive amount of her capital to achieve the certainty she required. This left her with a significant “surplus” of both capital and time and, crucially, the mental freedom to be more ambitious.

Finding focus within Global Health Alice turned to her aspirational goal around Global Health. While the research she and Bob conducted (Insight 2) was inconclusive about stakeholder preferences, it did highlight a global tendency to underinvest in prevention. This insight became the backbone of her impact focus.

The cost of a lack of focus Bob, in contrast, kept all his capital in one pot, managed for the vague goal of “more.” Without a clear financial goal, he felt constant anxiety and that he never had “enough” to pursue his own passions, leaving them as forgotten 38

Mission hedging

FOR MAKING HARD TRADE-OFFS COHERENTLY

FINANCIALLY HEDGING FUTURE IMPACT NEEDS

A strategic approach that recognizes and deploys all forms of capital—economic (money), social (networks), cultural (knowledge), and symbolic (reputation)— to accelerate progress on positive environmental and social impact goals. For instance, using your reputation to convene stakeholders, not just your bank account to fund them.

The practice of making the relative importance of an investment’s impact characteristics explicit by expressing it in a common unit, such as a rating or a monetary value. This enables better management of trade-offs and informed decision-making. As explored in Insight 3, it can be a powerful tool.

Like the reservoir overflow system shown above, a mission hedge is designed to create capacity when adverse conditions arrive. This means holding investments that are likely to perform well when your mission becomes more urgent. It’s about ensuring you have more resources available when they’re most needed. For example, holding semiconductor stocks if you worry about funding AI policy work, diagnostics investments if you worry about the next pandemic, or inflation-linked bonds if you support low-income households and worry about high inflation.

For Alice, this is no longer a theoretical exercise; it’s a practical challenge. She’s now grappling with how to value her portfolio’s contribution to long-term, systemic change alongside more immediate, measurable outcomes. This includes considering synergies where the joint effect of a set of investments is greater than the sum of its parts. 43

INSIGHT

LEARN

Goals evolve

Your goals, values, and beliefs are not fixed; they are hypotheses that evolve with learning, experience, and a changing world. That’s not a failure of conviction; it’s part of acting thoughtfully over time. Clarifying your goals is not the end, but the beginning of a journey filled with discovery. This evolution happens on multiple levels. Your intrinsic goals—your most fundamental views on what makes a good life and a better world—will likely change over time through philosophical reflection, exposure to new ideas, and profound life experiences. More frequently, your instrumental goals— the practical strategies and rules you use—will be updated based on new information and direct feedback from your actions.

This reality calls for humility, experimentation, and taking small, informative steps. You don’t have all the answers upfront, so it is important to learn in ways that keep your options open and reduce the cost of being wrong. As impact pioneer Jed Emerson notes, this is a two-way street: as you work to change systems, those systems, and your engagement with them, will inevitably change you.12

Insight 6

The value of impact goals

Even if you don’t currently have explicit impact goals, it can be worth exploring them. Beyond the direct good they can do for the world, they are also often good for you and more robust than personal desires. They expand your opportunities, opening up new ways to use your capital and talent. Personal desires can often trap us in a narrow set of games —whether chasing status, mimicking influencers, or pursuing things that aren’t possible in our current context. In contrast, the range of opportunities to help others is vast. The world is a big place; if your goal is to contribute, you will almost certainly find many opportunities. Furthermore, these opportunities will often be “low-hanging fruit” that are more effective ways to seek fulfillment than alternatives. This isn’t just a feeling; research shows that philanthropy can be a source of significant well-being for many people.13 A core problem with using wealth as a measure of success is that there are always wealthier people, which can leave you feeling dissatisfied. But if you use helping others as a measure of success, then it is natural to applaud and appreciate those who do even more. This creates a positive feedback loop: the act of contributing reinforces your sense of being enough (see Insight 1), which in turn unlocks an awareness of additional opportunities to contribute. 50

The Knowledge Illusion: why we never think alone The humility required for this journey rests on a simple truth: we all know far less than we think we do. In their book The Knowledge Illusion, cognitive scientists Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach show that human intelligence is fundamentally collective.14 We thrive by drawing on the expertise and perspectives of others. This humility brings us full circle to Insights 1 and 2. Because our knowledge is collective, our goals evolve best when we work with other stakeholders to clarify shared goals and manage our differences. True stewardship isn’t about knowing everything yourself; it’s about building a learning system that evolves with the world. For investors and philanthropists, this is why engaging with peers, listening to beneficiaries, and learning from communities of practice are essential for making effective decisions in dynamic environments. See the Investor’s Guide to Multicapital Strategies and the Investor’s Guide to Systemic Investing for further discussion.

Executive Summary This is a guide for investors who want to change the world. It supports investors in developing an evidence-based impact strategy for their entire portfolio. Here is a summary of our key messages and recommendations. WHAT IS INVESTOR IMPACT? Investors have impact, whether they mean to or not. By investing in corporations, investors might principally seek a financial return, but they are implicitly and explicitly also participating in the impact of their companies on employees, communities, and the planet. Increasingly, investors are embracing that role, desiring to create change in the world through their investments. But understanding the social and environmental impact of an investment is not as easy as simply investing in the most responsible company you can find. Your investor impact isn’t the impact of the companies in your portfolio. Rather, it is the change you induce through your investment in the impact of those companies.

The challenge is to separate the impact of the company on the world from the impact of your investment, in other words, to recognize two distinct components of impact:

Investor impact is the change in company impact caused by investment activities.

Company impact is the change in the world caused by company activities.

Organizations: CSP, University of Zurich
Publication date: 2021-09-23
Publication status: final

HOW CAN I HAVE INVESTOR IMPACT? Investor impact can mean enabling green companies with a net-positive impact to grow faster or encouraging “brown” companies with negative (or less than optimal) impact to improve. It can also include influencing other investors by being part of a movement. Thus, based on the available evidence, we make three recommendations on how you can maximize your impact as an investor:

Enable impactful companies to grow. • Typical asset classes: private equity, private debt, and venture capital • Allocate capital to young impactful companies in inefficient financial markets, as much as your risk-bearing capacity allows. Ensure the “additionality” of your investments by choosing companies that really need your capital and cannot easily get sufficient funding from other investors. • Consider investing in companies that require flexible or concessionary financing to scale their positive impacts. This will broaden your range of options, as many impactful companies cannot grow with financing provided at commercial terms. • When selecting fund managers, consider their capabilities to boost the growth of companies with non-financial support (e.g., their management skills, reputations or networks).

Encourage improvement. • Typical asset classes: public equity and debt • Vote your shares and engage with the management of all of your publicly traded equities. You can either interact with companies personally, get a service provider to do it for you, or select a bank or asset manager who does it. Whichever route you choose, the keys are to focus on realistic but meaningful improvements and to track outcomes. • Screen your public equity and debt holdings for transparent ESG criteria. Screening out companies that lag behind on widely accepted business norms (e.g., no child labor and setting climate goals) is more likely to cause companies to improve than screening out entire industries. • Focus on specific issues that are supported by a large coalition of investors and demand changes that companies can implement at reasonable cost.

Influence the public discourse by being vocal about what you do. • Be vocal about your investment decisions and why you made them. This can be a signal to other investors and to society at large. • If you are divesting from harmful industries, communicate this publicly. Divestment may support broader political or cultural change, but only when it is done publicly. • Enter coalitions with like-minded investors to join forces.

About This Guide This guide provides practical advice on how to have impact as an investor, based on a synthesis of academic research. More and more, investors want to drive positive change with their investments. This has brought new perspectives to investing and new products and services to the sector. Indeed, as more financial institutions promise impact in their offerings – from ESG ratings agencies to impact investing funds to shareholder advocacy groups – investors are finding it challenging to evaluate which strategies truly deliver on their promises. This guide supports impact-driven investors in developing an investment strategy that accomplishes real-world change. Changing the world through investing is complex and has been studied by many academic researchers. We’ve reviewed existing research,1 examined the mechanisms researchers have identified,

and synthesized the available evidence in order to offer these practical recommendations on how to maximize your impact as an investor with an evidence-based investment strategy. Importantly, while there are already many resources that focus on assessing the impact of investee companies, this guide is focused on the impact of the investor herself. Thus, we aligned the guide as much as possible with an emerging framework established by the Impact Management Project (IMP), a broadly supported initiative to manage and measure the impact of investments.

This guide makes several contributions to complement existing tools and approaches:

1 2 3

We clearly define investor impact, along with a rationale for why investors who want to change the world should focus on it. We detail a framework to qualitatively assess different mechanisms for investor impact, and their requirements and limitations, based on the evidence. We apply our framework to common types of sustainable investing products, with concrete evaluation criteria that investors can use to compare them.

The guide concludes with a suggestion on how to turn insight into action, as well as with a recognition of knowledge gaps. Research on the impact of investing is ongoing, and the recommendations in this guide may change as new knowledge becomes available. For now, however, this guide provides the best advice we can give.

What Is Investor Impact? Investor impact is the change that you cause in a company’s impact. Three key insights explain why. The impact of an investment is not as clear-cut as the prospectuses of sustainable investing products make it seem. That’s because it’s not accurate to simply claim a company’s impact as your own. A company might be doing well by doing good, but your investment only had

an impact at the margins, if at all. To truly get at what difference you made, you need to consider three insights that, when considered in turn, help to explain where and how your investment can do the most good.

INSIGHT #1:

Impact is change in the real world that is caused by your activities The idea of impact boils down to two things. First, something needs to change. Second, this change must be due to your activity, and not due to something or somebody else. Our simple definition for impact is this: Impact is the change in a specific social or environmental parameter that is caused by an activity. • Change: Having impact requires that something changes in the real world. There are many things you might want to change, for example, has there been a reduction of greenhouse gas emissions? Or an increase in the number of people with access to safe drinking water? To measure impact, you need to observe whether a set parameter is changing over time.

•  Causality: Having impact requires that an observed change is caused by your activities, and not by other factors. It’s crucial to think about what would have happened in absence of your activity (i.e., the “counterfactual”). Would the amount of people with access to safe drinking water have increased anyhow? Your impact is the change going beyond what would have happened even without your actions. This aspect of causality is also referred to as “additionality” or “contribution.”

WHAT HAS HAPPENED BECAUSE OF THE ACTIVITY

INSIGHT #2:

Your impact as an investor is the change in company impact that you cause. If impact is change caused by your activities then, as an investor, you do not directly have an impact on real-world outcomes such as global carbon emissions. But you may have an impact on a company, and that company has an impact on the real world. Thus, it is helpful to distinguish investor impact from company impact.

Investor impact is the change in company impact that is caused by an investor’s activity. For example, enabling a company to sell more products that reduce carbon emissions.

Company impact is the change in a specific parameter caused by company activities. For example, selling products that reduce carbon emissions.

Figure 3: Investor impact is about causing change – not about owning impactful companies. For example, investing in a company with a negative impact, and convincing it to improve (Brown Company) can result in a larger change than investing in a company that already has a net-positive impact (Green Company).

A common fallacy for investors – in terms of impact goals – is to assume that the company impact of their holdings is synonymous with their own impact. This can be misleading. To see why, consider the example illustrated in Figure 3. There is a green company with a net-positive company impact and a brown company with a net-negative company impact. Only looking at company impact, investing in the green company seems more attractive. However, if the green company has the same impact one year later, the investor impact was zero. When an investment in the brown company causes the company to reduce its negative impact, the investor had impact, even though the brown company is still far worse than the green company. So, to assess investor impact, investors must look at the change in company impact they cause.

Example: Does investing in pharmaceuticals make people healthier? Unfortunately, investor impact and company impact are often conflated. As an example, consider a self-proclaimed “impact mutual fund” that invests in public companies that contribute to the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) as defined by the United Nations. One of the fund’s top holdings is Gilead Sciences, one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world. Gilead develops and produces drugs for severe diseases, such as HIV. One might reasonably argue that the company has a positive impact on SDG Goal 3, Good Health and Well-Being. The number of HIV patients treated with the drugs produced by Gilead Sciences would be a reasonable measure of company impact. However, investors seeking impact should ask themselves, “If I invest in this fund, will more HIV positive patients receive treatment?” The answer is unlikely to be, “Yes,” given that Gilead can easily access capital to pursue the projects that management decides to pursue. But the only way to really answer this question is to think through the mechanisms of investor impact.

INSIGHT #3:

Investors can change company impact by enabling impactful companies to grow or encouraging companies to improve. There are two fundamentally different types of investor impact. Investors can either enable the growth of impactful green companies or encourage the improvement of brown companies that have potential to improve. There are various mechanisms to achieve these types of impacts, but both types ultimately result in an increase of company impact.

ENABLING GROWTH Investors can have impact by enabling impactful companies to grow. For example, an investment in a start-up that has found a way to make solar panels more efficient could have a big impact if the company is struggling to raise the capital it needs to scale.

ENCOURAGING IMPROVEMENT Investors can have impact by encouraging companies to improve their company impact. For example, investors may encourage a large manufacturer of snacks to stop using palm oil linked to deforestation.

While our guide puts a strong emphasis on investor impact, it is important to look at company impact as well. But depending on whether you intend to enable growth or encourage improvement, you might look at company impact in different ways. Here, we explain how company impact is relevant and point to several tools that go into more depth.

CHOOSING COMPANIES TO GROW If you want to enable growth, focus on companies that have significant positive impact on people and the planet. It would be counterproductive to help grow a company that has some positive, but also lots of negative, impact. Also, the positive impact of companies can differ by orders of magnitude, so picking the right ones is crucial. What you would look for is a robust estimate of the overall level of a company’s impact. The Impact Management Project (IMP) provides a broadly endorsed framework on how to assess the impact of companies. This framework differentiates between five dimensions of company impact: What, Who, How Much, Contribution and Risk. The Contribution dimension is crucial: If a company does not cause any change above what would happen anyhow, all other dimensions become obsolete. The Global Impact Investing Network’s (GIIN’s) IRIS+ offers a comprehensive catalogue of indicators that can be used to assess company impact. In addition, several providers offer databases on company impact. A recent report by the DVAF, the Association of Investment Professionals in Germany, provides a useful overview of these databases.

CHOOSING COMPANIES TO IMPROVE If your goal is to encourage improvement, you want to focus on those companies that have the greatest potential for improvement. Rather than measuring the overall impact of the firm, you need reliable information on specific environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria.2 This enables you to evaluate which companies have room to improve and whether companies are indeed improving. The challenge is to find criteria that are actionable for the company, easily observable by outsiders and widely adopted by investors. ESG rating agencies provide information that can be used to identify improvement potential. The more detailed and industry-specific indicators used by the rating agencies offer suitably comparable criteria on, for example, a company’s greenhouse gas emission intensity in comparison to industry peers, or the company’s revenues coming from SDG-aligned product categories. Controversy assessments published by data providers are an additional data source that can complement the company’s own disclosures.

The Mechanisms of Investor Impact There are different mechanisms of investor impact. We assess the effectiveness of each mechanism based on available evidence and identify key requirements and limitations. There’s more than one way to make a difference through your investments. Our starting point is the Impact Management Project (IMP)’s classification of four mechanisms of impact (see Table 1), which we’ve mapped to current academic research and modified modestly. To be sure, we also use some different wording than the IMP.3

In the section that follows, we look at the effectiveness of the different mechanisms of investor impact. For each mechanism, we give a concrete example, discuss the existing academic evidence for its effectiveness, and review its key requirements and limitations, as summarized in Table 3.

Investor Impact Mechanism (based on IMP classification)

Description

Grow new/undersupplied capital markets

Allocating capital to impactful companies whose growth is limited by access to financing.

Provide flexible capital

Allocating capital to impactful companies that require flexible financing conditions to grow.

Engage actively

Signal that impact matters

Provide non-financial support

Provide resources beyond capital that enhance the growth of impactful companies (e.g., know-how, reputation, network).

Shareholder engagement

Encouraging management to improve as an active owner (e.g., management dialogue, voting).

Market signals

Sending price signals to the entire market that encourage improvement (e.g., screening based on ESG criteria).

Non-market signals

Sending signals to society at large that influence the public discourse on pressing challenges.

Table 1: The mechanisms of investor impact.

LEVELS OF EVIDENCE Theories about investor impact abound, so we compiled as much evidence as we could to separate theory from reality. We reviewed academic studies that have investigated the effectiveness of different investor impact mechanisms and placed them within the IMP classification. Assessing how much impact you will have with an investment is prone to uncertainty.

Description

Systematic reviews of the empirical evidence document a scientific consensus on effectiveness of the mechanism.

B: Empirical evidence

Empirical studies show that the mechanism has been effective in specific settings. Yet, it remains unclear how far these findings can be generalized.

C: Model-based prediction

Economic models predict that the mechanism should be effective under certain assumptions.

There are narratives that rationalize why the mechanism could be effective.

Grow New or Undersupplied Markets Allocate capital to impactful companies whose growth is limited by access to financing. Investors can make a difference by enabling the growth of impactful companies. One way to do that is to invest in profitable companies whose business models contribute to solving the world’s problems, but whose growth is constrained by limited access to external financing. This kind of impact is directly caused by an investor’s capital allocation decisions and is often referred to as additionality. Investors may even create this additionality without making concessions on riskadjusted returns. The mechanism is effective if the capital provided to a company causes the company to grow faster than it would have without this capital. The mechanism thus only works for companies that are restricted in their growth by their access to external financing.

EVIDENCE LEVEL: B. EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE A large body of literature shows that investors can promote the growth of companies under the right circumstances. Many studies make use of unexpected shocks in capital supply to a sample of companies. These studies identify the circumstances where such shocks affect corporate investment and growth – and under which circumstances they do not. REQUIREMENTS: 1. Investee companies need to have a netpositive company impact so that a company’s growth results in greater positive impact. 2. Investee companies’ growth needs to be limited by access to external financing. This is more likely for small and young companies, for companies with a lot of intangible assets, or for those in immature financial markets, such as in developing countries. This does not mean that every young company in a developing country is restricted in its growth; investors would want to assess conditions on a case by case basis. LIMITATIONS: There is no empirical support for investors’ capital allocation influencing the growth of large, established companies. These companies usually have sufficient access to capital markets and are more constrained in their growth by product demand and competition than by access to capital. This is why the mechanism is oriented toward growing new/undersupplied markets. TYPICAL ASSET CLASSES: • Private equity • Private debt • Venture capital

Example: Bill Gates investing in Impossible Foods Meat production is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and the subject of ethical concerns. In 2011 Stanford biochemistry professor Patrick O. Brown started Impossible Foods to tackle this challenge. In 2013, Bill Gates invested 25 million US dollars in Impossible Foods – at a time when the prospects of the company were still extremely uncertain. Besides relishing the prospect of a handsome gain should Impossible Foods complete an initial public offering or IPO as expected in 2020, Gates arguably made a vital contribution to Impossible Food’s impact by enabling its rapid initial growth.

This example shows that investments have the highest potential to enable impactful growth where financial markets have the highest frictions – for example, due to the high level of information asymmetries and uncertainty of investments in early-stage start-ups. But it’s also important to consider that not every start-up is limited in its growth by access to capital. By now Impossible Foods has demonstrated its potential and many investors stand ready to invest additional capital.

The venture is now experiencing commercial success and has had an impact on carbon emissions and animal welfare. When Burger King rolled out an Impossible Burger across the United States in 2019, artificial meat entered the mainstream.

Provide Flexible Capital Allocate capital to impactful companies that require flexible financing conditions to grow. Growth may also be constrained not by access to capital per se, but rather by access to capital at the right price. Some impactful companies cannot grow with financing provided at commercial terms, so investors might provide them growth capital with flexible conditions. Companies whose business models resolve externalities not priced by the market (think cleaning up pollution where polluters don’t have to pay) or that focus on bottom-of-the-pyramid customers instead of more profitable market segments are less attractive to capital markets. There are different ways investors can offer beneficial financing. For example, they can accept below-market risk-adjusted returns, take subordinated debt or equity positions, or accept longer terms before exit. Investors offering flexible capital can also help companies steer clear of mission drift by lowering the pressure that capital markets often impose on growing companies to sacrifice impact for income. The additionality of a flexible investment, i.e., whether it has a causal effect on growth, needs to be assessed on a case-by-case basis. For example, it is important to make sure that the investment is not crowding out other sources of capital, including philanthropic capital or other impactoriented investors.

EVIDENCE LEVEL: B. EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE A range of empirical studies shows that flexible capital provided by governments, multi-lateral agencies and philanthropies have enhanced companies’ investment and growth. Several studies argue that private investors can promote impactful growth by providing similarly flexible capital. REQUIREMENTS: 1. Investee companies need to have a netpositive company impact so that a company’s growth results in greater, positive impact. 2. The investee companies need to be limited in their growth by a lack of access to flexible capital. This requires two things. First, a company needs to have sufficient opportunities to grow, given the right financing. Second, flexible capital makes a difference only if a company is unable to grow with market-rate financing. LIMITATIONS: The main drawback of this mechanism is that investors may need to compromise on riskadjusted return compared to non-flexible investment opportunities. This may not be an option for all investors – either due to their financial preferences or due to requirements related to their fiduciary duty. TYPICAL ASSET CLASSES: • Private equity • Private debt • Direct investments

Example: Root Capital financing the Musasa Coffee Cooperative Most smallholder coffee farmers in rural Africa sell their raw beans to local intermediaries and receive only a fraction of the coffee’s value-add. Connecting farmers directly to global specialty coffee markets can increase the farmers' revenues and thereby substantially improve their living conditions. Yet, producing for global markets requires large production volumes and expensive equipment and machinery, representing substantial upfront capital expenditures. This is a crucial hurdle for most smallholder farmers, as they do not have access to commercial sources of credit.

This example shows that capital allocation may have the strongest effects where financial markets are weakest – and that investors may need to be able to make a cut in their risk-adjusted return expectations to reach these places.

The nonprofit social investment fund Root Capital covers this gap and provides loans to coffee farmer cooperatives, like the Musasa Coffee Cooperative in Rwanda. Since Root Capital's initial investment in 2004, the number of farmers exporting their coffee over the Musasa Cooperative has grown more than fivefold. The loans provided by Root Capital generate positive returns. However, these are below the market rate for comparable commercial investments.
